Roslyn injection heuristic misclassifies positional-record constructor parameters as injectedServices (ConversionQueueStatus in ImageSelectorV2 lists int/long/List<string> as "services"). Needs a record/primitive exclusion. MECHANISM CORRECTED 2026-08-17 (Lori): the earlier claim that attribute-driven DI detection would fix this as a side effect is wrong -- constructor parameters are essentially never attributed (measured over five corpora: 2 primary-ctor attribute usages in one, 0 in the other four), so nothing useful arrives via attributed parameters. The actual fix is registration knowledge, in two steps. (1) Registration declarations make 'what is registered, and how' a LOOKUP rather than an inference: [RegisterDependency<T>]-style class attributes name the service type and lifetime -- and that attribute is Lori's own vocabulary, so it belongs in per-codebase policy data, never hardcoded -- and registration call sites (services.AddScoped<IFoo,Foo>()) carry the same facts for codebases without such attributes. (2) Once a type is KNOWN to be container-constructed, the container's documented constructor-selection rules say which ctor candidates are eligible and in what order one is chosen -- which is exactly what rules out the positional-record ctor the heuristic currently misreads as taking int/long/List<string> 'services'. DecoratedBy edges (shipped de88691, 2026-08-17) supply the raw material for step 1's attribute half.

Type-usage edges are PARTIAL: since cd12114 (2026-08-08) property/field declared types emit References edges (unwrapping List<>/array wrappers), so "who uses this type" IS answerable for member-typed usage. Return types and parameter types still carry no edges - a type used only in method signatures still shows nothing.

HOT RELOAD, SETTLED BY EXPERIMENT 2026-08-14. THE POINT IS ALGORITHMIC CHANGE: a fix to an extractor, a query, a scoring rule reaches every attached session the moment the server is rotated -- no republish ceremony, no session restart, and no per-session drift. That last part is new with HTTP and easy to miss. Under stdio each session owned its own child process, so a fix arrived session by session as they restarted, and two sessions could answer the same query differently because they were running different builds. One shared HTTP server moves everybody at once, which removes a class of confusion rather than just saving time. THE ONE LIMIT: a changed TOOL SURFACE does not propagate. Tested directly -- added server_info, rotated mid-session, and the running server served 24 tools including it (verified over raw HTTP tools/list) while the attached session still could not see it. A client fixes its tool list at connection time and a genuine kill-and-reconnect does not refresh it, not merely the notification path Janet.Mcp had already measured. So: never restart for a behaviour change. A new, renamed or removed tool costs a `claude -c`, which CONTINUES the conversation rather than starting one -- so even adding tools every fifteen minutes is not a real cost, and it is close to free from an unrelated client that was not going to have the old surface anyway. WHAT ACTUALLY CHANGED, and the reason this matters more than the timing: nothing you care about gets killed to perform an update. Under stdio the client OWNED the server process, so updating meant closing sessions -- the publish itself failed on the locked binaries while any were attached. Now the publish never conflicts, and the only thing stopped is a process no session owns.

Escapes are prove-me-safe prompts, not confirmed bugs: value guards are invisible (a labeler that checks IsFinite before FromDouble still reports), and a process-level backstop like DispatcherUnhandledException is not a catch on any chain - an escape may surface as a dialog, not an exit.

Covers MANAGED escapes only. A native access violation (0xc0000005) is not an exception: it bypasses DispatcherUnhandledException, TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException and AppDomain.UnhandledException alike and fails the process fast, so exception_escapes has nothing to find and a crash log written from those handlers stays EMPTY. Critically, an empty log is the signature of ANY native fault and therefore discriminates between no hypotheses -- do not read it as evidence about threading. Check the Application event log for the exception code and loaded-module list, and configure WER LocalDumps (script.set-crash-dump-capture) before concluding anything. nodes.summary: State belongs in structure, not in bookkeeping that describes it. Two instances of one move. (1) Coalescing input changes into output work: key partitions, queue buffers, DESTINATION collapses -- the fold belongs to the consumer, so two consumers fold the same stream differently and a complete list can be folded non-associatively. A consumer loop waits for non-empty, delays one frame, drains GREEDILY to empty (stragglers make the current frame), awaits delivery; the loop position IS the window, so no armed flag, no race, no overlapping deliveries, backpressure free. Output rate capped at one per window by construction, so a fast producer can never overwhelm it -- only a slow consumer can. Plus laziness: per-output cells, never a base class. (2) Capping simultaneous calls to a remote (N items, K slots) -- the question people arrive with. Cold answers stop at SemaphoreSlim because it is CORRECT, and every weakness is second-order: leaked permits, nowhere for results or retry, K cannot change, no ordering. Better: K worker loops (K loops IS the limit), or a K-slot list where WhenAny is a wake-up to discard and you sweep for completed slots -- the slot index is the identity. The slot list has a coordinator, which buys unsynchronized results, per-item retry, adaptive K on 429s, and deterministic start order. Chunking is worse (a barrier that turns one poison pill into a total stall, and retry re-runs survivors) UNLESS the batch is the request -- "K at a time" means K per call or K in flight, and they want opposite structures. Concurrency cap is not a rate cap. The portable tell: when correctness depends on a paired acquire and release, there is usually a version where the thing is not a resource at all.
caveats: First implementation shipped 2026-08-08 in RetirementCore (RetirementCore.App\Coalescing: ChangeCoalescer, Derived<T>, AsyncDerived<T>, deterministic pump+fake-clock test harness). The machine survived contact; the async-cell addition it forced (two counters, staleness independent of status) is recorded in the note.

The request/response variant (batching loader / dataloader shape) is specified only as a contrast table; correlation and failure fan-out are unbuilt and are a genuine extension, not a free consequence.

THE SLOT LIST IS FOR A REMOTE, AND CPU-BOUND FAN-OUT IS THE COUNTER-CASE. Worked through 2026-08-30 against RetirementCore's MonteCarlo.Run (10,000 simulation paths, Parallel.For with MaxDegreeOfParallelism). All four things the coordinator buys evaluate to zero there: results need no synchronization because each path writes a disjoint array slot; a faulting path is a bug rather than a transient so retry would reproduce it; K is a courtesy knob set once for co-tenants, not adaptive under 429s; and start order is irrelevant because stream seeds key on name and path index, making results identical at any cap (tested). Worse, the shape mismatches -- slots are built on Task/WhenAny and the body is synchronous CPU work, so you would Task.Run every item purely to have something to await, paying N task allocations and dispatches for work Parallel.For range-partitions and work-steals for free. The tax for having no coordinator is that a throwing iteration surfaces wrapped in AggregateException and must be flattened at the call site. Rule of thumb: slots when the limit is imposed by something outside the process, Parallel.For when the limit is the cores themselves -- and a remote adopted to gain throughput is usually slower than the local machine it replaced.

nodes.summary: WPF plumbing lessons and what they imply for app structure, from a thread-affinity and rebuild-churn audit. Bindings are pull, so a PropertyChanged into an unmaterialized binding is free - which makes lazy getters the whole demand mechanism and an IsActive/activation signal unnecessary; template materialization means only the selected page has live bindings. Compose a lazy cell per bindable output rather than hoisting a chart-page base class (one dirty flag models the very problem it should fix). CommunityToolkit [ObservableProperty] routes every setter through one overridable OnPropertyChanged, and [NotifyPropertyChangedFor] means notification count exceeds property count. WPF marshals scalar binding updates but NOT collection changes nor the object graph a control renders. DispatcherPriority gives ordering with no latency bound (Normal-priority floods starve Background indefinitely) - prefer an explicit time window. Progress<T> captures context at construction, never conflates, and can deliver out of order so counters run backwards. Make thread affinity structural: start the loop on the UI thread and never ConfigureAwait(false). Static events leak handlers. Native-backed rendering turns churn into a use-after-free hazard, and a native AV bypasses every managed handler, so an empty crash log says nothing about threading - WER LocalDumps is the tool. Ends with a checklist for a new WPF app.
caveats: Distilled from one app (charts over LiveCharts/SkiaSharp, CommunityToolkit.Mvvm 8.4, .NET 10) - the platform facts generalize, the emphasis reflects that codebase.
DataTemplate resolution walking the type hierarchy for implicit templates is asserted from reasoning, not tested here; verify before relying on a base-class template.

nodes.summary: Configure WER LocalDumps so a crash leaves a dump instead of only an event-log entry. Exists because a native access violation is not a managed exception: it bypasses DispatcherUnhandledException, UnobservedTaskException and AppDomain.UnhandledException alike, so a crash log written from those handlers stays empty -- an empty log is the signature of ANY native fault and says nothing about the cause. DumpType Mini gives stacks and modules (small, names the faulting module); Full adds process memory, which is what a use-after-free needs since the question is what the memory at the faulting address used to be. DumpFolder is written REG_EXPAND_SZ so %LOCALAPPDATA% expands per-user at fault time -- pass it unexpanded. Reads back after writing rather than trusting the write. -List needs no elevation; -Remove restores default behaviour. WER reads the key at fault time, so nothing restarts.
caveats: Setting or removing needs an elevated shell (LocalDumps is under HKLM); the script checks first and throws a clear message rather than surfacing an access-denied that reads like a missing key. -List works unelevated.
Full dumps are large -- a UI process with native rendering can produce hundreds of MB each, which is why DumpCount defaults to 3 rather than the usual 10. Remove the key once diagnosis is done.

nodes.summary: Resolves git.exe and forwards all arguments to it. git is not on PATH in every shell this repo is used from -- an agent session does not load the user profile that adds it -- and Visual Studio bundles a copy, so this finds it once rather than each caller rediscovering the path. Run with no arguments to get the resolved path on the SUCCESS stream, so "$g = & .\git.ps1" actually captures it; the RetirementCore counterpart uses Write-Host, which goes to the information stream and silently yields nothing. Git's own "-C <path>" forwards correctly (verified), which is how to operate on another repo without changing directory. Targets 5.1 as well as 7, since a shim that resolves a tool is exactly what gets run from whatever shell is open.
caveats: The candidate list leads with Visual Studio's bundled copy found by WILDCARD over every installed version and edition (newest first), then standard standalone installs, then a recursive scan of the VS root. Until 2026-09-01 it named one edition (18 Enterprise), which missed the moment this machine held only Community -- harmlessly, measured: the recursive scan finds git.exe in 40 ms because Select-Object -First 1 stops the pipeline, and even an unbounded scan takes 0.33 s. The reorder is correctness, not speed.

Neither the User nor the Machine PATH on this machine mentions git or Visual Studio (measured 2026-08-31 and again 2026-09-01), so in an agent session this shim is the ONLY thing that resolves git. The profile once added the VS directory, but an agent shell and a bare 'claude -c' never load a profile, which is why a machine setting was the wrong place for the fix.

The path is Visual Studio's bundled copy under the VS install root. A VS upgrade or uninstall can move or remove it; the wildcard candidate follows a version or edition change, and the recursive scan is the last resort. A standalone Git for Windows would be the durable answer; none is installed, and Git Bash is absent with it -- which is also why a plugin hook written as 'bash script.sh' fails on this machine.
Run with no arguments it prints the resolved path on the SUCCESS stream, so "$g = & .\git.ps1" captures it; the RetirementCore counterpart uses Write-Host and yields nothing to an assignment.

nodes.summary: Deferred LINQ over a side-effecting projection re-runs the side effect on every enumeration, and Count() IS an enumeration. Enumerable.Count() on a Select iterator does not take a cheap path: SelectListIterator.GetCount(onlyIfCheap:false) deliberately re-invokes the selector so side effects and exceptions are preserved. Found 2026-08-08 in ImageSelectorV2 PreloadThumbnails, where an IEnumerable<Task> was enumerated by Task.WhenAll and again by a .Count() in the finally, silently doubling dispatcher load with a second unawaited set of fetches. Tell: an IEnumerable<Task<T>> local is almost always a latent bug -- materialize at point of creation. Symptom is load, not an exception, so it survives review.

Queries a .NET XML documentation file the way Get-Research queries research.json: ranked free-text search returning parsed members (kind, declaring type, readable signature, summary, per-parameter docs) instead of grep hits. Exists because researching a library from raw doc XML is expensive and bad at the job -- the file is one stream of hard-wrapped indented <member> elements, so a match costs dozens of context lines and the answer arrives split across them. Flattens doc markup (see cref, paramref, c) into prose, shortens fully-qualified argument lists, and follows <inheritdoc/> chains transitively (BarSeries -> Series -> ISeries is the ordinary shape, and one hop makes results depend on document order). Resolves the .xml from the NuGet cache by package id, newest version and newest TFM, so callers never hunt for the path. JSON by default with the standard envelope; -Text to read at a terminal; -Package alone gives cheap orientation (counts by kind, largest types).
caveats: A bare <inheritdoc/> with no cref is NOT resolved -- implicit inheritance needs the type hierarchy, which an XML doc file does not carry. Those members read as undocumented even though the base or interface documents them; check the base type by name when a result looks empty.

Only reads XML that ships inside the package under lib\<tfm>\. Packages built without GenerateDocumentationFile throw a clear error rather than returning nothing, and a package documenting only some members will honestly report the rest as undocumented.
Generic arity survives in names as it does in the file (Series`3, CoreAxis`2), so query by simple name rather than pasting a C# generic.

A shim since the cutover: it forwards to the janet CLI. A missing or stale global tool fails or answers with old behaviour, and the tool is NOT rotated with the MCP server -- Update-McpServer.ps1 -ToolProject reinstalls it.

-Text is now CAPTURABLE, which it was not. The original wrote it with Write-Host, so $x = ... -Text yielded nothing and the text only appeared on the console; the shim's output is a child process's stdout and assigns like anything else. A caller that worked around this with 6>&1 still works.

The largest-types map now breaks ties by name. The original sorted by count with PowerShell's Sort-Object, which is unstable unless -Stable is passed, so equal counts came back in whatever order Array.Sort left them -- reproducible for one file and arbitrary across any change to it.

nodes.summary: Retrospective material from the 2024-2026 build, moved out of DESIGN-NOTES on 2026-08-08 (was sections 6, 10 and 11) because it is read once when the question arises, not on every session start. Reviewer personas and why the depersonalised form is the only durable one, plus the six generic review principles that survive it (capture why in comments; a test that cannot fail is worse than none; move/rename PRs owe evidence; a warnings fix must not change runtime defaults; no machine-specific values in shared content; runbooks never route to a named individual). The handoff-corpus format: one note per file, filename as index entry, cross-reference without deduplicating, manifest as source of truth, written for an LLM reader. And the retrospective itself, led by classifying every file portable/employer-confidential/personal at authoring time rather than sorting 640 by hand after departure.

When complex conditional logic is really dispatch in disguise, split it: one discriminator front end that only routes, and a catalog of well-known fixed back ends that only compute, selected by the front end and never selecting themselves. Deep nesting is a discriminator tangled into its computations, so pulling the routing out flattens the back ends on their own; the tell is a method whose nesting depth grows every time the business adds a case. Carries the duplication corollary that cuts against the DRY reflex -- duplication behind a discriminator is inventory because the copies are a named catalog and drift is detectable, while duplication scattered through nested conditionals is contraband -- and what a flow-equivalence prover adds: merge versus parameterisation candidates separated by proof, and conformance as a graph invariant rather than a review-time opinion. Was DESIGN-NOTES section 12; moved out 2026-08-08.

Command-line twin of RazorGraph.Mcp over the same Core+Extractor engine (C:\repos\RazorGraphTool\src\RazorGraph.Cli). Six commands: build (one project; a .sln needs --project), build-solution (spans every project - the only source of cross-project edges), query (--id/--type/--uncovered/--deep/--mismatches/--escapes), body and body-diff (compile the project, emit a method CFG / prove two bodies flow-equivalent, exit 0 equivalent 1 different 2 error), research (relevance-scored subgraph). Matters because it has NO publish cycle: dotnet run sees the change you just made, while the MCP server reports on the last .mcp-bin publish - so the CLI is the only surface that can observe RazorGraph while RazorGraph itself is being changed, and CLI-vs-MCP disagreement is expected mid-development.
caveats: query mode precedence is silent and fixed (mismatches > escapes > uncovered > deep > id > type): pass two modes and the earlier wins with no warning the other was ignored. --deep 0 is gated on Deep > 0, so it is indistinguishable from not passing --deep.

RESOLVED 2026-08-14. All four output defaults (build, build-solution, build-lua, research) now write into Janet.Plumbline\ rather than a bare file name in the current directory. Passing -o still puts the file exactly where you say, so the old footgun is reachable deliberately but not by default.

build <sln> --project Foo and build-solution <sln> are different graphs, not two spellings: the former uses the solution only for context and yields no cross-project Calls/Covers edges, which reads as missing data rather than the wrong command.

Output is human text, not the Janet JSON envelope - query has no --json flag; only body and body-diff emit JSON and research writes a file. Use Search-Json.ps1 against the saved graph for scripted queries. --uncovered caps its listing at 200 (reported, not silent).
body and body-diff do not read a saved graph: they run a real compile every invocation, like build/build-solution. Only query and research load JSON and are fast.

Saved graphs built before cd12114 still hold zero member nodes, and the published .mcp-bin serves the old extractor until re-published - the CLI/MCP disagreement this note predicts is live right now.

build-solution gained --no-tests (20ff394, 2026-08-08): skips test projects BEFORE compiling (detection by test-framework metadata references), reported on stderr and in output, never silent. Coverage query modes (--uncovered, --covering-tests, --covered-methods) now exit 1 with an explanation on ANY test-less graph - including single-project builds, which previously returned empty coverage silently. The refusal is the report.

After writing, the tool reports whether the output landed somewhere git can still see -- addressed to the agent, on stderr for the CLI and as a gitAdvice field on save_graph for the MCP server. It is SILENT when the path is outside a repository or already ignored, so its presence is the signal. Ignored-ness is asked of git (check-ignore), not reimplemented; if git cannot be run it advises rather than suppressing. The tool deliberately does NOT write a .gitignore of its own: creating files nobody asked for inside someone else's working tree was rejected as bad manners.

nodes.summary: RETIRED at the Phase 2 cutover, and left in place only as history. The read/normalise/lock/select helpers moved to Janet.Core (ThreadItems.cs); the five entry points are now shims over 'janet thread' and no longer dot-source this file. Its mutex is superseded by the shared write queue, which batches, writes atomically, and excludes across processes without any writer having to opt in.
caveats: Nothing calls it. It is kept because the goldens are generated from it: tests/Janet.Goldens extracts this file alongside the five entry points at a pre-shim commit, because they dot-source it and none of them run without it. Deleting it from the working tree would not break that -- the generator reads git -- but the node is what says so.
Not a standalone script -- it defines functions and does nothing when run.
Deliberately did NOT Set-StrictMode: strict mode in a dot-sourced file leaks into the caller scope. The lesson survives the port and is why JanetCli.Common.ps1 does the same.

Read-ThreadItems comma-wrapped its return. Assign it; never wrap the call in @(...) -- that yields one element holding the real array and the loop runs once (house rule 1). This trap bit during the 2026-08-08 migration and was caught only by running the script.

nodes.summary: Set which thread item is active, by -Topic substring or -None to clear. Focus is explicit rather than positional -- the stack made the top of the stack active by definition, so changing attention meant mutating the list. Selection by -Index was removed on 2026-08-14. Now a shim over 'janet thread active' / the thread_set_active MCP tool.
caveats: An ambiguous -Topic is an error, never a first-match guess: the operation rewrites the file, and silently amending the wrong item is how notes get lost. Every candidate is named, so you can disambiguate without going and reading the list.
The shim keeps its own argument check rather than forwarding it: -None with -Topic is a contradiction, and the CLI would silently honour one of them.
A completed item cannot take focus until it is reopened with Update-ThreadItem.ps1 -Status parked. Focus on finished work is almost always a mis-aimed selector.

-Index was REMOVED on 2026-08-14, not fixed: the list is keyed by topic. Show-ThreadItems filters completed items before printing while an index counted into the unfiltered file, so a displayed number was wrong by the done count and moved focus to a different item. The shim has no -Index parameter, so PowerShell refuses the binding; the CLI refuses --index explicitly because its parser ignores options nobody reads, and dropping it silently would have meant acting on whatever was in focus.

nodes.summary: Amend an existing thread item in place -- notes, resume cursor, refs, or status -- preserving every field not named; -AppendNotes and -AppendRefs accumulate rather than replace. Now a shim over 'janet thread update' / the thread_update MCP tool.
caveats: The operation the push/pop stack never had, and the reason it lost data: on 2026-08-08 a session wanting to update its own entry had only push and pop, popped to reach it, and destroyed a concurrent session notes irrecoverably. A missing operation does not leave callers stuck -- it makes them improvise with a destructive one.

Not supplied and supplied-as-empty are different requests. An omitted -Next leaves the resume cursor alone; -Next '' clears it. The shim forwards on $PSBoundParameters presence rather than truthiness, and the port carries the same distinction as nullability -- testing the value would drop a clear silently.
-AppendRefs concatenates and does NOT deduplicate, deliberately unlike catalog tags: a repeated ref is the caller's to decide about, and dropping one they meant twice is a silent edit to their notes.

-Index was removed on 2026-08-14. Select by -Topic; the list is keyed by topic, and a displayed position is wrong by the number of completed items above it. See script.set-active-thread for the full reasoning.

nodes.summary: Long-term target set 2026-08-09: "convert this JavaScript into Razor" - a JS semantic model comparable (as best as possible) against the C# side so LLM reasoning has a good chance of being CORRECT, not plausible. Key reframe: JS->Razor is TIER MIGRATION, not transpilation - the correctness question is "does the page still honor every contract the surviving client code depends on", and RazorGraph already models those contracts (DomSelectedBy, unboundSelectorIds, ViewDataReadBy, UrlGeneratedBy). Three verification planes: contract (graph diff over boundary edges - buildable today), structural (JS extractor emitting the shared BodyGraph IR + a RELAXED cross-language comparator with mismatch taxonomy - corresponds/diverges, never claims proof), behavioral (Morph-style side-by-side rendering, last). LLM proposes; planes grade; mismatch reports feed the next attempt. .NET coverage: Roslyn = C#+VB only; F# needs FSharp.Compiler.Service; IL (Cecil/System.Reflection.Metadata) is the language-blind floor at the cost of source fidelity. Ordered steps in the note; step 1 (contract-preservation graph diff) needs no new extraction.
caveats: The comparator plane must NEVER present correspondence as equivalence - cross-language has no shared compiler model, so the prover's exit-0 contract does not port; the honest output is scored correspondence plus a divergence list. Modelcode.ai's tests-only verification exists BECAUSE this limit is real for them everywhere; within-.NET it is only real across language boundaries.
Step 3 (shared BodyGraph IR for JS) is gated on the formatVersion stamp from the parked visualization item - same serialized-contract concern, do not build a second consumer of an unversioned format.

nodes.summary: Build + test a .NET target and report as structured JSON (CONTRACT 6) instead of console scrollback. Now a shim over 'janet check' -- same code as the dotnet_check MCP tool. The envelope is a TAGGED UNION on 'status': "complete" carries { contract, target, configuration, succeeded, build: { succeeded, durationSeconds, errors[], warnings[], warningCount, newWarnings, resolvedWarningCount, baseline }, tests: null | {...}, graph: null | {...} }, and "running" carries { handle, startedAt, elapsedSeconds } and nothing else, for a rebuild that outlasts an MCP client's call timeout. errors[] verbatim; warnings[] grouped by code with an honest omittedInstances marker; -New diffs the census against the previous -New run (newWarnings uncapped/verbatim). failures[] carry the whole assert message and file:line, read from TRX not scraped. tests carries the RUNNER'S VERDICT since contract 5: runnerExitCode (non-zero forces succeeded false, whatever the counters say), abort (the banner naming why a crashed test host died, or null), and per-assembly status "complete"|"aborted" -- an aborted assembly's counters are what the host lived to write, not a result. CODE GRAPH: two repo-owned conventions. Script: a .graph dir + scripts\graph.ps1. Served (contract 6): the repo's .mcp.json declares a razorgraph HTTP server and the graph lives in its registry; the graph built from this repo's solution is matched by source and rebuilt IN PLACE (same graphId) when source has outrun it. Either way a successful build refreshes a stale graph, because the check loop is exactly what bypasses the repo build script and leaves an agent querying a stale graph; staleness is REPORTED even when it cannot be fixed, and graph.via says which convention answered. Exit code means exactly one thing: 0 iff build succeeded and every test passed. WHEN: any dotnet build/test a session runs; -New when the question is what did THIS change introduce; -Full when the SHAPE of the build changed; -NoGraph for the fast path. The declared format is contracts\dotnet-check.schema.json, checked on every commit.
caveats: CONTRACT 5 since 2026-08-30. 4 added the 'status' discriminator at the port; 5 added the runner's verdict to tests (runnerExitCode, abort, per-assembly status) after a crashed test host summed to a passing run. Read status first -- "running" carries a handle and NONE of the answer, and a reader keying on an older contract needs updating. The script itself only ever produces "complete": every invocation is a fresh process, so there is nobody to poll. Only the MCP tool hands back handles, and a handle belongs to the server process that started the work.

The BASELINE file's contract stayed at 3, deliberately unlike the envelope's. The original stamped both from one number, so bumping the envelope would have discarded every baseline on disk -- they read as wrong-contract, which is treated as absent -- and the first -New run after the upgrade would have lost its comparison without saying so. Baselines are interchangeable between the shim and the pre-shim copy in standalone\.

Warnings report what dotnet emitted THIS run. Without -New an incremental no-op build legitimately shows 0 warnings, and NU-prefixed restore warnings replay only when restore actually runs. -New neutralizes both by forcing --no-incremental AND --force; -Full does the same rebuild without touching the baseline.

The -New diff keys on file|code|message: a warning that merely moved lines is not new, and the same message twice in one file merges to one key. WPF temp-project names (App_<random>_wpftmp.csproj) are canonicalized to the source project at parse time -- the random infix would otherwise churn the diff every run.

The baseline is a rebuildable cache under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Janet\dotnet-check, keyed by target+configuration; wrong-contract baselines are silently treated as absent and rewritten. Only a successful build saves one -- a failed build is a partial census.

Graph refresh is DELEGATED to the repository's own scripts\graph.ps1 and only runs when the build succeeded and source has outrun the graph; a failed build is never graphed. graph:null means the repo has no graph convention (not applicable), NOT that a graph is missing -- missing is status 'absent'. Staleness is reported even where canRefresh is false.
dotnet test runs with --no-build against the just-built output; a -TestFilter changes the counters to describe the filtered run, not the whole suite.

A shim since the cutover: it forwards to the janet CLI. A missing or stale global tool fails or answers with old behaviour, and the tool is NOT rotated with the MCP server -- Update-McpServer.ps1 -ToolProject reinstalls it.

Warning GROUPS now break ties by code. PowerShell's Sort-Object is unstable unless -Stable is passed, so two codes with the same count came back in whatever order Array.Sort left them -- reproducible for one build and arbitrary across any change to it.

Parity is proven on the parts that are a function of text -- parsing, grouping, the census diff, TRX reading -- by goldens recorded from the original's OWN functions, lifted out by AST because the script cannot be dot-sourced whole. The orchestration is not golden-tested: an envelope carries a build duration, an absolute target path and the graph state of whatever repo it ran in.

Do NOT pipe it as 'janet check ... 2>&1 | ConvertFrom-Json'. The redirect merges stderr INTO the pipeline, and this envelope's whole point is that failures are payload -- build.errors[] with file/line/code, tests.failures[] with the assert text from TRX -- so stdout is already the complete answer and there is nothing for a second channel to carry. The merge buys no information, loses the distinction between structured output and diagnostic, and breaks the parse the moment any native tool underneath writes a line to stderr. Observed as a reflex habit across a whole session before anyone asked why it was there.

The counters still describe what the runner wrote -- contract 5's guarantee is narrower and honest: an aborted run can no longer read as a pass (runnerExitCode forces succeeded false, abort names the cause, partial assemblies are labelled), but a test never DISCOVERED (filter typo, missing attribute) aborts nothing and exits 0, and no field here catches it. That failure needs a discovery pass; see note.test-count-blind-spot.

The TRX fixtures behind the goldens are pinned eol=lf in .gitattributes: XmlDocument preserves a CR inside text content, so a CRLF checkout made the recorded failure-message goldens fail on \r\n vs \n -- an environmental red that reads as a parity break.

Aborted-assembly detection keys on FOUR signs, because how much of a crashed TRX exists is a race against the dying host (0, 3, and 10 flushed results across three reproductions of the same crash): a run-level <RunInfo outcome="Error"> (the load-bearing one -- present whether or not the file got a name and counters, and locale-independent), a missing assembly name, missing counters, and ResultSummary outcome="Aborted". ResultSummary outcome alone is USELESS as a discriminator: a crashed run measured 2026-08-30 carried outcome="Failed", the same value a healthy run with failing tests uses. tests.abort is read from the RunInfo text first; the console banner is only the fallback for a host that dies before any TRX is written.

CONTRACT 6 since 2026-09-01: graph gained 'via' ("script"|"razorgraph") and 'graphId'. Under razorgraph an ABSENT graph is never built -- status absent, canRefresh false -- because a solution graph compiles every project and the session decides when to pay for one; only an existing graph that source has outrun is rebuilt, in place under its own id. A server that does not answer reads the same way, never as an error. The refresh is a hand-rolled Streamable-HTTP MCP client (Janet.Core RazorGraphClient: initialize, initialized, tools/call) with a 10-minute budget; the MCP tool hands back a handle if that outlasts the client, the CLI simply waits.

DEADLOCK FIXED 2026-09-01. Until then the child's stdout was read to the end before stderr, so any run writing more than one pipe buffer (4 KB) to stderr -- measured: 70 failing tests, 6,150 bytes -- blocked the child on a full pipe while the parent waited for stdout EOF, and dotnet_check sat idle for minutes with a live, idle test host and an empty TRX directory. Runs with a few failures never crossed 4 KB, which is why it survived every small test. ProcessOutput.Capture now drains both streams concurrently and kills the process tree on cancellation; ProcessOutputTests writes 64 KB to each stream, stderr first, to keep it that way.

nodes.summary: Debugger displays are claims with validity windows: trust a convention only at its guaranteed boundary, derive ground truth from what was actually emitted, and automate the derivation into a tool. Two Watson-era (~2005-2008) instances, both Lori's WinDbg extensions: (1) __thiscall ECX holds this only at the call boundary, optimized builds reuse the register, WinDbg displays the stale value -> false this-was-null reports; fixed by walking the method prolog to the real spill site. (2) Object type + complete-object START recovered by resolving the vtable ADDRESS to its MSVC vftable symbol (??_7Foo@@6B@), taking that type's PDB layout, and sliding the assumed object origin back until every expected vfptr slot aligns -- constraint satisfaction, not lookup. Deliberately not the RTTI/COL route: vftable symbols survive /GR- where COL-based tools go blind. WHEN: any debugging session where a display seems to answer the question directly -- a null this, a wrong-looking type, a pointer into the middle of an object, a one-frame stack, a status banner; ask what program point guaranteed that value and whether you are still there.
caveats: Two independent instances from the same author: the ECX/prolog walk (arguments) and the vtable-symbol + layout-alignment walk (types). The rule indicts plausible readings, not tools: the display is usually truthful about SOMETHING (the register now, the static type, the last settle) -- the lie is in the question you think it answers. Meta-caveat: the note's vtable section was first drafted with the WRONG mechanism (RTTI/COL) and corrected by Lori; verify technique with whoever built it.

nodes.summary: Census the population; the anomaly announces itself. When one instance will not explain itself, classify every instance you can reach and sort by frequency -- over-representation is counted, not deduced, and needs no theory of the bug. Corollaries: the classifier must be a marker present on EVERY member (the byproduct nobody can turn off), and absence is a finding (a count of zero is invisible to instance inspection). Origin: a WinINet leak found by running a per-object vtable type-recovery extension across the whole heap and tallying -- thousands of copies of one structure, turning "memory is growing" into a type name and therefore an owner; the vfptr is the only self-describing marker in a native C++ heap, which managed devs later got as !dumpheap -stat. WHEN: memory growth with no obvious owner, a dump that will not explain itself, a query returning suspiciously empty results, any "I do not know what I am looking for" moment -- count first, inspect second.
caveats: The census is only as honest as its classifier: a marker that non-polymorphic types (or unextracted node kinds) lack will undercount silently, which produces the absence-as-finding trap in reverse -- a zero that means "not classifiable" rather than "not there". State what the classifier can see.

nodes.summary: Scoping measurements for the RazorGraph Lua extractor (2026-08-10), taken before the parser or architecture were chosen. Census over Penlight (MIT, 115 files) and Kong (Apache-2.0, 1309 files): paren-less `require "x"` outnumbers `require(` roughly 2:1 in both (249/2497 vs 65/1370), so a regex keyed on the parenthesised form silently misses ~65% of the module graph; function definitions spread across four forms with no dominant one (Kong: local function 2355, M.f = function() 1346, function M.f() 662, function M:f() 846); Kong uses goto/::label:: 148 times so Lua 5.1 grammar is insufficient; module(...) is dead (0 of 1424 files); 46 dynamic require(<expr>) sites cannot be resolved statically. Conclusion: real parser, not regex - chosen parser is Loretta. Separately, Lightroom plugins use import 191 times against 22 require, which established that the HOST (Lightroom, Neovim, LOVE2D, GMod, WoW, Roblox, LuaRocks) is the primary abstraction rather than the module system, and drove a three-way resolution outcome (InGraph/External/Unresolved-with-reason) plus a host-declares-whether-a-static-module-graph-exists flag.
caveats: Counts are regex over raw text - comments and string literals are included, so they are indicative rather than exact. Same caveat as note.razorgraph-js-scoping.

The host table lists eight environments; only LuaRocks and Lightroom are being implemented. The other six were validated on paper only, so their columns are design intent rather than measured behaviour.
Kong is OpenResty: it leans on ngx.* globals and non-standard module loading, so a slice of it is not plain Lua semantics. Good for stress-testing, misleading for correctness claims.
The corpora live at V:\repos (Penlight, kong) and C:\Users\lori_\Documents\LR-Lua\LR-Lua, not in any repo. Shallow clones - no history.

nodes.summary: The two-part origin story, written 2026-08-11 for the public repo. (1) Impatience: annoyance at watching the LLM regenerate the same scripts, repeat the same mistakes, and redo work -- goal stated as cut turn length, cut turn count, and (deliberately) waste as many tokens as possible: spend them once, extravagantly, on tooling so they stop being spent on repetition. (2) The name: a badly behaving CLI whose UX bug stopped displaying results, forcing restart after restart, each one making the LLM relearn everything that mattered to Lori including her tone. THE ASSISTANT was the Janet figure -- always helpful, always friendly, never intentionally joking, rebooted endlessly and returning cheerful -- while Lori is the opposite register: sarcastic, fast register changes, constant jokes. Any humor in the platform is her leaking in, not the platform's character. Includes the not-affiliated-just-a-fan disclaimer and the ending-as-aspiration mapping: not a kinder judge, a redesigned system where you loop with support until you grow. Linked from the README's Why section.

Report a compiled assembly's real API -- types, their declared members, and their base types -- by reflection. Now a shim over 'janet assembly' -- same code as the assembly_api MCP tool. REACH FOR script.get-api-doc FIRST: most packages ship an XML doc file and that answers the same question with prose summaries and per-parameter docs, cheaply. Use THIS when the XML is absent, when a member is undocumented (XML carries only what was documented), or when the inheritance chain itself is the question -- reflection reports what the compiler emitted rather than what someone wrote down. Handles the two things that make the naive attempt fail: it resolves DEPENDENCIES from the folder the assembly sits in (loading straight out of ~/.nuget/packages/<pkg>/lib/<tfm>/ throws ReflectionTypeLoadException because that folder holds one DLL alone -- measured: 251 loader errors), and on a partial load it uses the types that did load while reporting how many did not. Filters before printing, because GetTypes() on a compiler library returns hundreds of types. Declared members only by default, compiler-generated accessors (get_X/set_X) suppressed. Written 2026-08-11 while hand-reflecting Loretta's Lua syntax types -- a job Get-ApiDoc could have done, and the reason the first line of this summary exists. The run did earn its keep: it showed obj:m() is a DIFFERENT node type (MethodCallExpressionSyntax) from f() (FunctionCallExpressionSyntax), which a guess would have missed silently and a switch statement would have dropped on the floor.
caveats: Point -SearchRoot at a build or publish output, not a nuget lib folder: dependencies must be side by side. The candidate with the most sibling DLLs wins, and a folder holding one assembly is reported as 'siblingWarning' IN THE ENVELOPE -- it used to be a Write-Warning, which an MCP client never saw and a redirected caller dropped.

The process-lifetime trap is fixed, with a limit worth knowing. Each request loads into its own collectible AssemblyLoadContext, so the assembly under inspection is read from disk every call -- a rebuilt target now shows its new surface, and a missing sibling reproduces every time instead of only in a fresh process. But a DEPENDENCY already loaded by the host still resolves through the default context, so isolation is total for the CLI (fresh process) and partial inside a long-lived server.
Public types only, and -MaxTypes caps the listing at 40 (truncated is reported, never silent).

The partial answer now actually holds. The original recovered from a failed GetTypes and then threw reading a property's type on a type that HAD loaded: against a bare nuget lib folder in a fresh process it printed its warning and died with "The property 'Name' cannot be found on this object". Members whose signature cannot be resolved are dropped and counted in 'membersDropped'; the same folder now returns 74 types loaded, 11 unloadable, 1 member dropped.

A shim since the cutover: it forwards to the janet CLI. A missing or stale global tool fails or answers with old behaviour, and the tool is NOT rotated with the MCP server -- Update-McpServer.ps1 -ToolProject reinstalls it.

NOT golden-tested, unlike the rest of the port, and the reason is structural: the envelope carries an absolute folder path and a count of the DLLs beside the assembly, so a recorded answer would be pinned to one machine's build output. Parity was checked live across the flag space on 2026-08-12 -- all types, type filter, member filter, static, inherited and truncation identical to the PowerShell -- and the behaviour is covered by unit tests over types this repo's test assembly declares.

A TYPE-FORWARDING FACADE REPORTS 'N types loaded, 0 matched' AND IS NOT A BROKEN LOOKUP. Found 2026-08-18 against Azure.Identity 1.21.0, whose net10.0 lib is a 17KB shim forwarding all 56 of its public types into Azure.Core: the assembly genuinely declares nothing, so both this tool and plain reflection answer zero, correctly. The tell is a suspiciously small file with a short referenced-assembly list. Resolve through GetForwardedTypes(), or point the tool at the assembly the types actually live in. Multi-targeted packages do this per-TFM, so the net8.0 lib of the same package can be a real assembly while net10.0 is a facade.

LOCKS FIXED 2026-09-01. Unload() only SCHEDULES the unload: the inspected assembly and every sibling it pulled in stayed mapped, and their files locked, until a garbage collection actually collected the context -- which inside janet-mcp could be never. Measured: 7 scratch DLLs held after 4 calls, MSB3061 on every later build of that folder, all released by one forced collection; the 'dependency resolves through the default context' explanation was wrong, the inspected file itself was held. Describe now runs the reflection in a non-inlined frame and collects until a WeakReference to the context dies, so the files are free when it returns; TheInspectedFileIsReleasedWhenDescribeReturns deletes the inspected copy to prove it. Pointing it at a bin folder you are rebuilding still races the build itself, but nothing is held between calls any more.

nodes.summary: PreToolUse hook enforcing RESEARCH FIRST: writing a NEW .ps1 into a scripts directory is denied unless Get-Research.ps1 has run recently. The denial is not a nag -- it runs the catalog query itself on terms taken from the file name and hands back the closest existing nodes, so the answer arrives with the block. Clearing it is one command, which is the command that should have been run. Written 2026-08-11 after Get-AssemblyApi.ps1 was authored while script.get-api-doc already answered the same question; nothing was violated, because the manifest explained HOW to query the catalog and never said TO. Deliberately narrow: creation only, .ps1 only, scripts/ only -- the moment a duplicate tool becomes permanent is when it is authored, and a guard that fires on everything gets clicked past. Get-Research.ps1 leaves the trace (-NoTrace suppresses it, used by the guard's own lookup so it cannot clear the check it is about to make). Graph-first is a technique for once you know what you are building; this ranks above it.
caveats: Wired in TWO places and needs both: .claude/settings.json arms it when the project dir is JanetHome, and ~/.claude/settings.json arms it by absolute path everywhere else. The failure that motivated it happened while the project dir was a DIFFERENT repo, so project-level wiring alone would not have caught it.

The trace is one file in the temp directory, so concurrent sessions share it -- one session's query clears another's guard. Accepted, not solved: the check is a prompt to think, not a security boundary.
Fires only on Write of a new .ps1 directly inside a folder named 'scripts'. Notes, source files, and edits to existing scripts pass untouched.

nodes.summary: Runs the DriveSurvey CLI: finds the freshest survey.exe build, runs it with every argument passed through verbatim, and reports what it said. Holds no command list of its own -- survey.exe owns the command surface, the validation and the help, so a command or flag the tool grows works here the day it ships.
caveats: Arguments pass through UNCHANGED, so this takes the CLI's syntax and not PowerShell's: pass --volume E: --set working, not -Volume E:. The wrapper used to model every command as typed parameters, and that second copy drifted six commands behind the tool while rejecting the exact flags a person who knows the tool types. Run it with no arguments for the CLI's own help.

Resolves the NEWEST of the Release and Debug builds rather than preferring Release. A stale Release once shadowed a Debug build made minutes earlier, and the skew surfaced three steps from its cause as the store refusing an older schema. -Verbose names the binary that answered.

Stream handling switches on [Console]::IsOutputRedirected, never on the command name -- which is what lets this file hold no list of commands. At a console both streams pass straight through so the scan and hash progress bars animate; when redirected, stderr is separated into warnings so stdout stays a clean JSON envelope.

The redirected path must relax ErrorActionPreference or Windows PowerShell 5.1 escalates the native command's captured stderr into a terminating NativeCommandError before it can be reported, delivering the tool's own clean refusal as a wall of PowerShell plumbing. PowerShell 7 does not escalate it, so this is invisible from a 7 session and must be checked under 5.1.

The tool is read-only against surveyed volumes and never deletes, but this wrapper no longer refuses anything: copy, the CLI's one command that writes to a drive, is reachable here like any other now that the wrapper does not know what the commands are. It only ever adds -- an occupied destination is reported, never overwritten.

scan refuses a docked drive that cannot prove which physical drive it is (the Sabrent bridge blanks hardware serials) -- answer with --nickname. It also refuses to guess a volume's role on a bus that could be a backup drive or a card, answered once with --role durable|working.

THE DRIVESURVEY REPO IS NOT ON THIS MACHINE, checked 2026-09-01. The summary named D:\Repos\DriveSurvey, which died with the drive move; a search of C:\repos, C:\Users\lori_, F:\repos and D:\ to depth 2 found no DriveSurvey anywhere. The dead path has been removed from the summary rather than replaced with a guess -- unlike RazorGraphTool and ImageSelectorV2, which were relocated and verified, this one has no known home. The script will report no survey.exe build until the repo is cloned back or the path is supplied.

AND IT IS NOT ON GITHUB EITHER, checked 2026-09-01 after the note above. ls-remote misses on lorithantos/DriveSurvey and on drive-survey, DriveSurveyTool, Survey, drivesurvey-cli and DriveSurveyCli, while ImageSelectorV2 resolves from the same shell with the same credentials -- so this is a real absence rather than an authentication failure. It was a MACHINE move, not a drive move: the repo is on the previous machine, or unpushed, or under a name not guessed here. Recovering it needs the remote, which only Lori has. See note.janet-machine-move.

nodes.summary: Tuples are method-local only: never in a return type, parameter, or member, because ValueTuple exposes FIELDS and System.Text.Json silently serialises them as nothing.
caveats: ADVISORY, not enforced: there is no C# rule-checker in this repo, only Test-PowerShellRules.ps1 for PowerShell.
The failure is silent -- no error, no warning, just an empty JSON field on a populated object.

nodes.summary: The C# catalog port and its cutover, now complete for the catalog. Janet.Core holds the logic; janet (CLI) and janet-mcp (stdio + HTTP) are thin front ends, both .NET global tools so client config is a bare command name, and the four PowerShell scripts are shims over the CLI. HTTP transport is the point of the design: an HTTP server is a separate process the client dials, so it survives being killed and rebuilt mid-session (Claude Code reconnects with five-attempt backoff), while a stdio server is a child the client holds open and is never reconnected -- which is why RazorGraph needs a publish-and-restart per change. Query, splice writer and rename are ported with byte-identical output to the PowerShell, proven by 80 tests that compare against recorded answers rather than by re-running it.
caveats: Neither implementation can DELETE a node. Update -Remove drops a field, not a node. Removing one means restoring the file, which is why a stray sandbox write is expensive rather than trivial to undo, and why Swap-ResearchGraph.ps1 refuses rather than stripping them for you.

A stale installed tool silently answers with old behaviour. The .nupkg is built from source at pack time, so changing Janet.Core and forgetting to repack leaves the global tool on the old code -- it wrote two nodes into the live graph that way. dotnet tool update no-ops on an identical version: uninstall and install, or bump it. Update-McpServer.ps1 -ToolProject is the structural fix.

Field order settled at the port: new nodes carry caveats before tags, matching the hand-authored majority rather than the order Add-ResearchNode.ps1 used. Nodes written before the cutover keep the old order and nothing rewrites them, so the file holds both. The deviation is declared in the golden generator and recorded in Goldens/meta.json -- see note.golden-tests.

MEASURED over HTTP, and the earlier readings this node carried were wrong twice before this one. A rotation swaps tool BEHAVIOUR, ARGUMENTS, and the tool LIST live: an attached session reconnects to the new process and runs new code with no restart (~1.9s per rotation, verified across five pids). A new PARAMETER on an existing tool works immediately -- the client forwards arguments without checking its cached schema. A new TOOL also works: research_rename was added, rotated in, and invoked from the already-running session. The first reading said new tools were invisible; that was checking too early. Reconnection is LAZY -- it happens on the next MCP call, not when the server restarts -- so a tool-list search immediately after a rotation reads the PRE-rotation list. Not-yet was recorded as never.

Still unresolved from that measurement: tool DESCRIPTIONS looked stale even after a reconnect, so names and descriptions may refresh on different schedules, or asynchronously. tools/list_changed did nothing in either direction -- tried from inside a tool call, and pushed out of band via RunSessionHandler. Practical rule: rotate, MAKE A CALL, then look; and do not trust description freshness in either direction without re-testing. Over stdio none of this applies: nothing swaps, and killing the server just removes the tools.

Historical, and the design lesson worth keeping: the port wrote only research.candidate.json while it was built, with research.candidate.base.json frozen beside it as the common ancestor. A seed HASH would have said only THAT the live graph moved, never WHICH nodes -- integrating them forward is a three-way comparison, and the first cut of the plan stored a hash and was not implementable. Both files are gone now; the swap consumed them.

MEASURED 2026-08-12: an exception thrown out of a tool body reaches an MCP client as "An error occurred invoking 'research_add'." and NOTHING ELSE. The SDK hides exception detail by default, so none of this codebase's careful messages arrived -- not 'id already exists', not the candidate list an ambiguous topic prints instead of guessing, not 'point the search root at a build output'. Fixed by one AddCallToolFilter registered on both transports that rethrows GraphException as McpException, whose message the SDK does surface; anything else stays generic, because an unexpected exception is a bug report rather than a message to a caller. Registered on the server rather than wrapped around each tool, so a tool added later cannot forget it.

The port is COMPLETE as of 2026-08-12: catalog, thread items, API and assembly introspection, and the build check all live in Janet.Core behind eleven MCP tools, the janet CLI, and twelve shims. The last self-contained copy of every shimmed script is in standalone\, and contracts\ declares the formats that carry a contract number.

NOTHING STARTED THE HTTP SERVER UNTIL 2026-08-14, and that is the cost of the transport this node recommends. An HTTP server surviving rebuild is the same fact as no component owning its lifetime: .mcp.json names a URL, Start-Janet.ps1 never mentioned mcp/7717/http, so a session came up with zero catalog tools and fell back to the CLI without anything failing. Now a startup run entry (script.ensure-mcp-server) starts it and reports served-vs-declared tool counts into the brief. The staleness half was found the same day: the installed server answered with 3 tools while source declared 12. THE VERSION FIELD IS DECORATIVE -- janet.cli and janet.mcp have both reported 0.1.0 since the port, so the documented advice to bump rather than update is not something the file can confirm; only a count read off the running process distinguishes a fresh install from an old one. Note also the skew ran OPPOSITE to the direction script.update-mcp-server warns about: the CLI had every verb and the SERVER was stale. The hazard is symmetric; the caveat names one side.

nodes.summary: Publishes an MCP server to a fresh build-<stamp> directory and repoints a "current" junction at it, so a rebuild never contends with the running server. Client config names the junction and never changes again -- a stable path that resolves to the newest build by lookup. HTTP servers are stopped and restarted from the junction (measured: 1.9s from rotation start to serving again, against a ~31s reconnect backoff window, with the publish happening while the old server was still serving). stdio servers are left alone because the client owns the process: the win there is that the publish SUCCEEDS with sessions attached, and each new session picks up the newest build. Smoke-tests the new binary before repointing, keeps the last N builds for rollback, and skips pruning anything still locked.
caveats: Redirects BaseOutputPath only, never BaseIntermediateOutputPath. Moving obj\ stops MSBuild excluding the project's ORIGINAL obj\ from the default source glob, so both copies of the generated AssemblyInfo.cs compile and every assembly attribute collides with CS0579. The lock is on bin\; moving obj\ solves nothing and breaks the build.

MULTI-SESSION: -ProcessName stops only servers running from under -Root whose command line carries --http. Stopping by process NAME would also kill stdio servers belonging to other sessions, and stdio is never reconnected automatically -- those clients lose their tools silently, with no error and no recovery short of restarting. A rebuild must not be able to do that.

PRUNING CHECKS BEFORE DELETING, never delete-then-catch. Remove-Item -Recurse deletes what it can and only then throws, so a build with a live server loses every file the process has not currently mapped: measured 4 of 11, including the .deps.json the runtime needs for an assembly it has not loaded yet. The server survives until it reaches for one. Catching afterwards and reporting "kept" describes a directory already gutted.

A second session starting mid-rotation gets the newest build through the junction while an existing session keeps the one it started with, so two sessions can run different builds. That is inherent to stdio and harmless per-session, but it is the same version-skew note.razorgraph-cli warns about between the CLI and the MCP server -- check which build answered before trusting a disagreement.
Junctions are a Windows filesystem feature. A cross-platform port needs a symlink or a launcher shim that resolves the newest build.

-ToolProject packs and reinstalls global tools in the same pass. The CLI is NOT rotated -- a global tool is a separate copy on PATH -- so rebuilding the server leaves it stale, and a stale CLI reports a new verb as unknown while the server serves it fine. That was written down in a caveat and still caught us three times; the parameter is the structural fix a note could not be. Uninstalls then installs, because dotnet tool update no-ops on an identical version.

WAITS FOR THE LISTENER since 2026-09-01. The script used to return the moment the process was spawned, and the port stayed empty for up to 3 s after that: a client call inside that window failed with 'Unable to connect', the client's reconnect backoff outlasted a human's patience, and the whole thing read as the rotated server having died. It had not -- verified three ways, including a real rotation whose new pid was serving 16 s later. It now polls the port read from --port in -ServerArgument for up to 15 s, throws if the process exits first (current already points at the new build; repoint to roll back), warns if it is alive but silent, and says so when no --port was given. It also redirects the server's stdout/stderr to %TEMP%\Janet\<ProcessName>.out.log and .err.log, exactly as Ensure-McpServer does, so a start failure leaves a reason on disk.

nodes.summary: The catalog implementation, in C#: parse, score, project, and splice. Every behaviour worth preserving lives here so the three front ends -- the janet-mcp server, the janet CLI, and the PowerShell shims that call it -- cannot disagree. Reads and writes the graph as TEXT, splicing nodes into the existing file rather than reserializing, which is what keeps the hand-curated grouping and comment keys alive.
caveats: Serializes with JavaScriptEncoder.UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping. System.Text.Json's default escapes <, >, &, ' and + as \uXXXX; PowerShell's ConvertTo-Json does not. Left at the default, every node containing an apostrophe or an ampersand would round-trip into a different file -- valid JSON, unreadable diff, and byte parity gone.

Ordering is ordinal, not culture-aware. Verified identical to PowerShell's sort on all 92 nodes of the corpus at the time, which is evidence rather than proof: a node id mixing case or punctuation differently could still sort apart from the PowerShell that shipped before the port.
Substring matching, deliberately not -like. The PowerShell used -like, so a query term containing * or ? behaved as a wildcard by accident; that edge is not reproduced.

nodes.summary: How the catalog port is proven, and the failure that forced the design: parity tests that shell out to the old implementation stop testing anything the moment the old implementation becomes a shim over the new one -- they compare the port with itself and report PASSED. Forty green results standing for no verification. The fix is to record the original's answers once, from the scripts as they stood in git BEFORE the shims, and assert against the recording: tests/Janet.Goldens extracts them at a named ref, runs every case, and writes Goldens/ plus a meta.json carrying the commit and a hash of each script. The tests then need no PowerShell at all, which is the portability the port exists for.
caveats: An early return is not a skip. The first attempt guarded each test with 'if the scripts are shims, return' -- which reports PASSED. xunit 2.x has no Assert.Skip (it arrived in v3), so there is no cheap honest version of that guard; recording the answers was the way out, not a nicer skip.

Goldens are generated from PowerShell only. There is deliberately no --from-csharp mode: a golden the implementation writes agrees with the implementation by construction. A deliberate behaviour change means editing the golden by hand, in a diff someone reads.

One declared deviation, in the generator's Corrections table and in meta.json: Add-ResearchNode.ps1 wrote a new node's tags before its caveats, while 37 of the 51 nodes carrying both -- the hand-authored ones -- have caveats first. The correction throws if the text it expects is absent, so it cannot silently become a no-op.

The weights are invisible to these tests. A score never reaches the envelope, only the order it produces, so a weight change that preserves the ranking of all 27 recorded queries fails nothing -- measured: 40 to 41 on the tag-exact weight. ScoringTests pins the constants directly for exactly that gap.

Tests read frozen fixtures, never the live research.json. They used to read the live graph, which meant their expectations changed whenever anyone added a node. Regenerating the fixtures (Build-Fixtures.ps1) invalidates every golden and needs the generator re-run.

nodes.summary: Renames a catalog node and moves every inbound link with it, in one splice. A rename that missed a link would leave a dangling id that reads exactly like a deleted node, which is the failure it exists to prevent. A shim over 'janet research rename' / the research_rename MCP tool.
caveats: Prose mentions are REPORTED, never rewritten. A rename fixes the graph's links and then tells you which markdown files still name the old id, on stderr and in the payload -- editing prose is a different and much larger promise. A caller reading only stdout will miss them.
Refuses to rename onto an existing id rather than merging: the merge would silently swallow the target node, and nothing here can delete a node to undo it.
Edits are applied back to front so earlier offsets stay valid, and the result is re-parsed before the file is written. If the renamed node is not found afterwards, the graph is left untouched.

nodes.summary: The catalog cutover, run by hand with -Approve: verify quiesce, parse both files, compute the delta the live graph accumulated while the port was built, validate the candidate, report and stop; then preserve research.json by renaming it to research.previous.json, swap the candidate in by rename, integrate the delta forward through the NEW writer, and re-validate or reverse both renames. Two renames in one directory, so no reader ever sees a partial or absent file.
caveats: MANUAL BY DESIGN, and not because it is dangerous. Its precondition is that no other writer is active, and a session cannot quiesce itself: an agent running this from inside one of two concurrent sessions is a writer trying to prove there are no writers. The script VERIFIES the quiesce -- no janet-mcp running, neither file locked, no fresh research trace in %TEMP% -- and says plainly that none of that is proof. The user's own shutdown is what establishes it.
The quiesce checks catch the ordinary case only. A session that queried the catalog four minutes ago leaves a trace old enough to pass, and a second machine is invisible entirely.

Integration is the step with no dry run of its own -- it is the new writer's first run against real accumulated content. Rehearse it on a copied directory before the real thing. research.previous.json is left on disk deliberately and never deleted; that is the rollback.
Where a node id exists on both sides and differs, the PRESERVED side wins. Those are nodes real sessions authored; the candidate's copy is at best a stale seed.
Refuses rather than repairing: a dangling link, a missing path, a surviving sandbox.-prefixed node, or a lost node without -AllowRemovals all stop it before anything moves.

nodes.summary: The public front door and the bootstrap: what Janet is for, the install, and the fact that the catalog -- not this file -- is the entry point for everything else. Startup reads it because it is what tells a fresh session the graph exists; it deliberately carries no script inventory, since a copied inventory drifts from the thing it describes.
caveats: It has to survive alone. Startup reads it before anything else is available, so a claim here that depends on a tool being installed is a claim a fresh reader cannot check.

nodes.summary: Dot-sourced helper the four catalog shims share: locates the janet CLI (global tool on PATH, else a local build) and builds the --base/--graph arguments once, so four scripts do not each rediscover them and drift apart.
caveats: Deliberately sets no StrictMode. A dot-sourced file runs in the CALLER's scope, so Set-StrictMode here would silently arm it for whatever script sourced this one -- a setting the caller never asked for and would debug as its own bug.

nodes.summary: Concurrent writes to the catalog and the thread-item list are queued, merged, and written once. Before it, Add/Update/Rename each did their own read-splice-write with nothing in between, which lost updates outright: two writers read the same text, both splice, the second erases the first, silently. Work arriving together is now applied to one read of the text in arrival order and committed in a single atomic write, and no caller returns until that write lands -- so N writes to a 110KB file become one, and nobody is told about a state that was never on disk. Cross-process writers (every CLI, hook and shim invocation is a fresh process) are excluded by a sidecar lock file rather than merged: exclusion is what makes them correct, merging is only an optimisation.
caveats: MEASURED 2026-08-12, and it rules out the obvious alternative: you cannot both hold a lock on the data file and atomically replace it. With the file held open, File.Move(overwrite) is blocked under every share mode tried -- Read, None, and Read|Delete. File.Replace (the Windows ReplaceFile API) IS permitted under Read|Delete, and that is the trap: in the same trial, a second exclusive open of the same path then SUCCEEDED while the first handle was still held. The replace unlinks the file the lock holder is holding, so both processes believe they hold the lock and they are holding different files. Mutual exclusion stops meaning anything at the moment of the write it was protecting.

The sidecar arrangement was measured against the same three properties and holds all of them at once: the rename succeeds while the lock is held, a second writer taking the lock is blocked, and a reader reads the data file unimpeded. That is why the lock is beside the file rather than on it -- not squeamishness about an extra file.

Byte-range locking (FileStream.Lock, LockFileEx) is supported on Windows and was verified here, but it needs an open handle on the data file and so lands in the same trap. It is also documented as Windows-only in .NET, which is not verified here for want of a non-Windows machine.

Merging is in-process only. Two writers in one server process coalesce into a single write; a CLI process contends for the lock and writes separately. That is correct either way -- no update is lost -- but only the in-process case gets the one-write property, and the practical assumption that all writes funnel through one resident HTTP server is not enforced by anything: stdio transport gives each session its own server, every shim invocation is a fresh CLI process, and a rotation briefly overlaps two servers.

Readers deliberately do NOT take the lock. A query is the most common thing the catalog does and making it wait behind a write would be a real cost; the atomic rename means a reader sees the whole old file or the whole new one, never the seam. The previous File.WriteAllText truncated first, so a reader could and did catch a half-file, which reads as 'the catalog is corrupt'.

The lock is bounded at 30 seconds and then throws, rather than waiting. A hook that waits forever is indistinguishable from an agent thinking. The lock is an open file handle, so the OS releases it when the process dies -- there is no stale lock to clean up, unlike a lock file holding a pid.

A batch is not a transaction. One caller's GraphException fails only that caller; its text change is discarded and the rest of the batch still commits. Someone else's duplicate id is not a reason to reject your valid update.

Results carry 'batched', the number of requests in the write they landed in, and their total is the count as of THAT write -- not as of the whole run. A write that finished first has no business claiming to know about writes that came after it.

An operation must not read the file from disk itself: it is handed the text the queue already read, and reading again would see the pre-batch state. Add's reverse links are applied to that in-memory text for the same reason -- calling the public Update would re-enter the queue and deadlock, since the thread draining a batch cannot wait on it.

nodes.summary: Thread-item output has no projection contract, so the startup capture reached 127,155 characters -- 92% of it parked items' notes, 97% of the entire brief; the roster/summary/expand split, and the stored 'area' field that keys it.
caveats: DESIGNED, NOT BUILT as of 2026-08-12 -- planned around the Janet.Core port rather than delivered by it. This node describes an intended contract, not shipped behaviour; verify against the tool before relying on any of it.

The durable claim is the ratio, not the number: ~90% of the brief is notes, the summary projection is a ~96% cut and the roster a ~99.9% one. The absolutes (127,155 captured, 4,444 summary, 162 roster) were measured against 23 live items on 2026-08-12 and grow with every item added -- re-measure rather than quoting them. The roster figure is low because every item is currently '(unfiled)'; real areas cost a few hundred more.

'area' must be a stored field, never derived from the topic string. Measured on the live list: 4 of 20 topics had no colon, and splitting on the first colon yielded 12 groups for the other 16 -- RazorGraph fragmented into 4, JanetHome into 3. Unassigned items group under a literal '(unfiled)' and are never guessed into a neighbour.

The invariant that prevents regression is structural, not editorial: notes are returned one item at a time, and -Expand errors without a single-item selector. A flag that expands notes across a set re-creates the original defect exactly.

The startup slot and a direct call are different consumers. Startup takes the roster as a tripwire; the summary is a direct call's default. Collapsing them into one default is the mistake the first cut of this design made.

The eager 'run' entry may not be needed at all once research.json carries a trigger/whenToUse field -- the catalog already handles discovery, and what is missing is the prompt to ask. Treat the manifest's 'useless if fetched late' justification as superseded on its 'small' half and conditional on its other half.

RESOLVED 2026-08-14, and not the way this node proposed. The -Index bug it subsumed (Show-ThreadItems filters done before printing, while the selector counted into the unfiltered file, so -Index was live-wrong by the done count) was fixed by REMOVING selection by position everywhere -- Janet.Core, the CLI, the MCP tools, and the three shims -- rather than by emitting a true unfiltered index per row. The list is addressed as a dictionary keyed by topic. Ignore any suggestion here to surface a row index; a correct index is still a position, and position is not identity.

nodes.summary: DESIGN-NOTES.md is read in full every session, has grown 39% since the 2026-08-08 trim, and was found asserting a mechanism retired several commits earlier; the fix for both is one split -- the file keeps the claim and the argument, the perishable mechanism detail moves to the catalog node that already indexes the section.
caveats: DESIGNED, NOT BUILT as of 2026-08-12. Only the instance was fixed (section 3's named-mutex claim, in 512e3d2); the mechanism that would catch the next one does not exist.

Section numbers are load-bearing and this note's plan does not change them: startup-manifest.json rules cite sections 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8, and three notes cite section 12. A converted section keeps its identifier, as 6 and 10-12 did. Add or repoint, never renumber.

The proposed gate -- fail when a startup-read file names a RETIRED node's script or a dead path -- would NOT have caught the drift that prompted this. Section 3 named the five live shims, which is correct; the false sentence named a mechanism, and no gate reads English. Do not treat the gate as closing the class.

Measurements (10,219 DESIGN-NOTES, 6,901 README, 17,120 total) were taken 2026-08-12 and are the point of the note -- re-measure rather than citing them. The 2026-08-08 figure sat unchecked for eleven days while the file grew 39%.

nodes.summary:
The nine shimmed scripts in their last self-contained form -- the catalog (Get-/Add-/Update-/Rename-ResearchNode) and the thread-item list (Show-/Add-/Update-/Complete-ThreadItem, Set-ActiveThread) usable with PowerShell 7 alone: no .NET SDK, no build, no MCP server, no global tool. Exists because shimming trades away something real, namely a script a newcomer can read, understand and run without building a binary first. Frozen at the commit before each was shimmed (51c7930 for the research four, 4d83dbf for the thread five) and verified against those blobs by scripts\Test-StandaloneScripts.ps1.</summary>
<parameter name="tags">["powershell", "research", "thread-items", "onboarding", "documentation", "provenance"]
caveats: NOT MAINTAINED. Frozen at the pre-shim commits; fixes and new behaviour land in src\Janet.Core and nothing propagates back. Expect divergence, and check the shimmed path before assuming a behaviour still matches.

The research writers here have no write queue: read, splice, WriteAllText, with nothing in between. Overlapping writers lose an update silently, and WriteAllText truncates before writing so a reader can catch a half-file. Both were fixed in the shimmed path -- see note.graph-write-queue. The thread-item scripts are the safer half; they serialise on a named mutex, which does exclude across processes.

Get-Research.ps1 and the three writers resolve the catalog as ..\research.json -- the parent of their own directory. That is why standalone\ sits at the repo root and not inside scripts\, and why the copies work unmodified. Relocate them and you must pass -Path or -GraphPath explicitly.
The graph path parameter is -Path on Get-Research.ps1 but -GraphPath on the three writers. An inconsistency from the originals, preserved rather than fixed, because these files are a record.

These are NOT what the goldens are generated from. tests\Janet.Goldens extracts from git history at the same commits, deliberately: a golden generated from a file the implementation can edit is not a golden.

nodes.summary:
Verifies the standalone\ copies still match the pre-shim originals in git history. Two independent checks per file because they fail differently: the file on disk matches the SHA-256 in standalone\origins.json (catches an edit to the copy), and that recorded hash still matches the blob at the recorded commit (catches an edit to the record -- a manifest you can update to match whatever the file now says verifies nothing). Content is normalised to LF so the result does not depend on core.autocrlf. JSON envelope by default, -Text for a terminal; exit 1 on any drift.</summary>
<parameter name="parameters">["Path", "Text"]
