caveats: The history check needs git. Without it the on-disk hashes are still checked and the envelope reports gitChecked:false -- read that field rather than only the exit code, because a check that could not run is not a check that passed.

Verified by mutation 2026-08-12, all three caught with distinct diagnoses: editing a copy reports 'edited', editing origins.json to match the tampered copy reports 'record-drifted', and deleting a file reports 'missing'.

Not wired into Test-PreCommit.ps1. Pre-commit gates on staged files, and these are frozen files nothing stages -- run this after a history rewrite, a filter-branch, or any operation that could move the recorded commits.

nodes.summary:
Holds a tool's output format to the schema checked in beside it under contracts\, and holds a schema change to being a deliberate one. Two checks, because format drift travels in two directions: SHAPE validates each schema against live envelopes (additionalProperties:false, so a field added to the code turns it red), and CHANGE requires that a schema differing from the reference commit also bumped its contract number AND changed the script that exposes the format. Samples the repo build rather than the installed janet. JSON envelope by default, -Text to read, exit 1 on any finding. Step 6 of Test-PreCommit.ps1, and only where a contracts\ directory exists.</summary>
<parameter name="parameters">["Path", "Against", "Text"]
caveats: The schemas are hand-written and MUST NOT be generated from the return type. A schema the implementation writes agrees with the implementation by construction, which is the same reason a golden the implementation writes is not a golden -- generating them would leave this script reporting a pass it never earned.

It samples the REPO BUILD (src\Janet.Cli\bin\...\janet.exe), falling back to the installed tool and reporting which one answered under 'sampledFrom'. Found by mutation: while it sampled the global janet every mutation passed, because that binary is whatever was last packed -- the staleness note.janet-mcp-port documents, arriving as a gate that could not fail.

A schema absent from the reference commit is exempt from the change rule: it is a NEW format, not a changed one. Demanding a bump from nothing, and a script edit the new format may not need, would make the gate fire on correct work -- and a gate that fires on correct work gets disabled.

Shape is only checked as far as the samples reach. One envelope does not exercise one schema: the samplers deliberately produce three, because a single unfiltered run never shows truncated:true and never reaches an enum. A schema branch no sample reaches is unverified, and the gate does not know that.

JSON Schema pins SHAPE, not MEANING. It cannot express that graph:null means 'not applicable' rather than 'missing', so the catalog caveats stay load-bearing and a passing gate is not a read contract.

Verified by mutation 2026-08-12, eight ways: a field added, removed and renamed; a kind spelled differently; the contract number moved in code only; the schema edited alone; the schema edited with a bump but no script change. All caught.

nodes.summary: Proves a test suite would actually catch the defects it claims to, by breaking the code on purpose and requiring the suite to go red. Takes a JSON plan of mutations (file, find, replace, optional test filter); per mutation it applies the edit, REFUSES ONE THAT CHANGES NOTHING, runs the suite through Invoke-DotnetCheck, requires failure and records WHICH tests failed, then restores from the bytes read before the edit and verifies the restore by SHA-256. A green baseline is required first (failures cannot be attributed in a suite that was already red) and a green final run is required last (which is what proves every restore landed). Exists because this repo already believes the principle -- pattern.reviewer-principles says tests must be able to fail, note.golden-tests records forty green results standing for no verification -- while every actual mutation check (Test-OutputContracts eight ways, Test-StandaloneScripts three) was done by hand once and survives only as a claim in a caveat. JSON envelope by default, -Text to read; exit 1 on any not-caught, no-op, unapplied or unrestored mutation.
caveats: IT EDITS SOURCE FILES IN PLACE. Restore is from an in-memory byte copy in a finally block and is verified by hash; a failed restore writes the original to <file>.mutation-original, stops the run, and says not to trust anything after it. Run on a clean working tree so git is a second way back.

A green result means the mutations you WROTE were caught. It says nothing about the ones you did not think of, and it is not a coverage tool -- an uncaught behaviour with no mutation aimed at it looks identical to a well-tested one.

The no-op guard is the load-bearing part and was written from a real mistake: a do { X } while (false) wrapper around an awaited call, authored as a mutation on 2026-08-14, is semantically identical to X. It passed, and the pass was briefly mistaken for evidence. A find/replace whose result is byte-identical now reports no-op instead of running.

A 'find' matching more than once is refused as ambiguous rather than guessed at -- measured on Controls.xaml, where the obvious setter text matched four times and a hand mutation would have silently broken a different style. Set occurrences to 'all' to mean every match.

Multi-line finds are literal, so line endings matter. These working trees are LF while git reports CRLF on checkout; a find written with CRLF reports not-found against an LF file, which reads like a wrong path rather than a wrong newline.

Relative paths in a plan resolve against the TARGET solution/project directory, not the plan file. Found by dogfooding: a plan written into a scratch directory resolved every path against the scratch directory and reported file-missing for all of them. Set "root" to override.

Runs the suite through Invoke-DotnetCheck, which shims to the janet CLI, so a missing or stale global tool makes every run unavailable rather than failing. That is reported as suite-unavailable and exits 1 -- read the finding kind, because a check that could not run is not a check that passed.

Dogfooded against Janet.Shared 2026-08-14: three real mutations caught with the exact test names (key filter -> 2 tests, coalescing window -> 3, cell alignment -> 1) and one deliberate no-op refused. The Janet.Shared working tree was byte-clean afterwards.

nodes.summary: Startup run entry that makes sure an MCP HTTP server is up, and reports what it is actually SERVING. Parameterised per server since 2026-08-31 (-Name, -BinDir, -ServerArgument, -SourceDir); janet-mcp on 7717 remains the default, and Ensure-RazorGraphServer.ps1 forwards to it for razorgraph-mcp on 7718. The HTTP transport is a separate process the client dials -- which is what lets the server be rebuilt mid-session, and also what means no component owns starting it. A session whose server is down does not fail: .mcp.json names a URL, so the tools are simply absent and the session falls back to the CLI, which works well enough that nobody notices. Emits compressed JSON: ok, state (already-running|started|not-running|not-answering|start-failed|no-server-binary|error), port, pid, serverPath, base, toolsServed, toolsDeclared, stale, note, error. Starts from the <BinDir> junction Update-McpServer.ps1 maintains, falling back to <Name> on PATH. -NoStart to probe only, -Pretty to indent.
caveats: GENERALISED 2026-08-31, and the defaults are what keep it compatible: omit the new parameters and it behaves exactly as the janet-only version did (verified -- identical 14/14 already-running output before and after). -Name drives the default executable, the log file names, and the remediation text; -SourceDir drives the staleness count; -ServerArgument replaces the argument list wholesale, which is REQUIRED for a server that does not take --base. razorgraph-mcp does not: it is told which solution to graph per call, not per process, so passing janet's default set would make it exit at startup.

NEVER THROWS, BY DESIGN -- it runs in the startup path, and a startup script that can take the session down is worse than the problem it solves (house rule 6). Read ok, not the exit code. Its failure reaches the brief as a captured run result, never as a problems entry, so it cannot block a launch: the CLI fallback is real, and refusing to start over a missing convenience would be worse than the fault.

The staleness check counts [McpServerTool( in -SourceDir (default src\Janet.Mcp) and compares it to what tools/list returns. THE PAREN IS LOAD-BEARING: matching the bare prefix also matches the [McpServerToolType] container classes, which inflated declared from 12 to 16 and reported a stale server that was perfectly current. That bug was written and caught during authoring, 2026-08-14.
toolsDeclared is null where -SourceDir is absent, and no comparison is made -- a deployment without source reports no verdict rather than a false one.

A live pid with toolsServed 0 is state not-answering, NOT already-running: something holds the port that does not speak MCP. Verified against a raw TcpListener. A plain TCP check cannot tell these apart, which is why the probe does the MCP handshake rather than testing the socket.

BOTH INTERESTING BRANCHES ARE NOW VERIFIED END-TO-END. Stale, 2026-08-14, by accident rather than by a contrived fixture: adding the thread_report tool took declared to 13 against a server still serving 12, the detector fired with stale:true, the remediation command it prints was run verbatim, and the next probe read 13/13. Start, 2026-08-31: razorgraph's server was killed deliberately, the port confirmed empty, and the script brought up a new pid from the junction serving 25/25.

Windows-only: Get-NetTCPConnection has no cross-platform equivalent here. Wrapped so a failure reports not-running rather than throwing, which on another OS would mean it starts a second server rather than finding the first.

The tool-count comparison catches a stale SERVER, not a stale CLI. The global janet is a separate copy on PATH and goes stale independently -- and it is what every PowerShell shim calls, so the startup brief can carry an older envelope than the repo build emits, with every gate green. See script.get-thread-report, where that was measured.

nodes.summary: The thread-item list as a MAP rather than as its contents: topics, focus, refs, next, and the SIZE of each item's notes -- without the note bodies. Answers "where was I", which is the question asked on resuming. Envelope is CONTRACT 1, declared in contracts\thread-report.schema.json and checked on every commit. Each item carries notesLead (first non-empty line, capped at 200 chars) and notesLength (full size); the envelope totals what was withheld, so the omission is stated rather than implied. Three front ends over one implementation, as ever: thread_report, janet thread report, scripts\Get-ThreadReport.ps1. Read one item in full with thread_show once you know which one you want. Startup runs this instead of Show since 2026-08-14, captured as threadReport.
caveats: A SEPARATE VERB, NOT A FLAG ON SHOW, and the reason is mechanical rather than aesthetic. Show's envelope is asserted byte for byte against output recorded from the pre-shim PowerShell, which tests\Janet.Goldens extracts out of git at a277625 and RE-RUNS -- so that envelope can never grow a field by regeneration, only by a declared correction to a contract with a live consumer. A new format beside it needed no correction at all, and all 216 existing tests stayed green. Test-OutputContracts exempts a schema absent from the reference commit from its change rule for the same reason.

THE SHIM CALLS THE GLOBAL TOOL, so the startup brief's shape depends on the INSTALLED janet, not the repo build. Measured 2026-08-14: the repo build stamped contract 1 while the global tool, packed minutes earlier from source that predated the field, emitted the envelope without it -- and Test-OutputContracts stayed green throughout, because it deliberately samples the repo build. The gate and the brief can therefore disagree. Reinstall with Update-McpServer.ps1 -ToolProject after any format change.

notesLead is the first NON-EMPTY line, not the first: notes built by appending begin with a blank line, so "first line" is empty for most items that have anything worth reading. Capped at 200 characters plus a trailing ellipsis.

Report reads THROUGH Show rather than beside it, so the two cannot disagree about which items are live, which is active, or how a corrupt list is reported. A test pins that agreement: if the cheap view and the expensive one ever diverge on membership, the cheap one stops being a safe substitute, which is the whole premise.

Measured on the 2026-08-14 list: 174,129 characters through Show against 26,613 here, and the startup brief 181,303 -> 30,457 bytes. thread_show on that same list EXCEEDED the MCP tool result limit and returned nothing usable, which is what prompted this. The saving is not uniform -- three items held a third of the total.

nodes.summary: Attribute census for RazorGraph's attribute vocabulary (2026-08-17), 8,047 usages over five corpora via Roslyn SYNTAX-ONLY parse (scripts\AttributeCensus.cs, exact not regex-indicative) -- and the method that let a scoping census graduate into a verification ORACLE: every shipped increment (DecoratedBy/Registers/Parameter/assembly, formatVersion 1.1) reconciled against exact expected numbers by a route independent of the extractor. Key findings: distinct attribute types are tiny (7-113) while usages are not; 50-80% is xUnit plumbing which is why payload suppression is policy data; parameter attributes are rare but pure signal (Parameter nodes emit only when decorated); ctor params are essentially never attributed (the DI fix is registration lookup + container ctor-selection rules, NOT attributed params); assembly attributes are an OrchardCore manifest story plus an obj\ generated-file trap (plain .cs, not .g.cs -- gate on the path segment); typeof/generic type arguments are ~0.5% of arguments and every one is a framework-constructs-this link (the Registers edge).
caveats: Counts are syntax-layer: exact over what syntax shows, but blind to what only the semantic layer decides -- record [property:] attributes land on the PROPERTY in the real extractor (2 in RazorGraphTool), and compiler-generated sources are compiled without being on disk (5), so a syntax census and a compile-based graph legitimately differ by exactly those; the note itemises the reconciliation.

Census scope must match BUILD scope before its numbers are an oracle: the whole-tree count was a wrong oracle for a .slnx build because tests\fixtures\ carried the repo's only ASP.NET attribute usages. Rescope, then reconcile.

KNOWN DEFECT: the corpus-declared matcher appends 'Attribute' to a name already carrying <>, so generic attributes never match the declared set -- ImageSelectorV2's usagesOfCorpusDeclaredAttributes reads 9, truth ~45 (40 field-verified). Per-target/per-type counts unaffected. Fix in scripts\AttributeCensus.cs before trusting that one split.

The script is a .NET 10 file-based app needing '#:property JsonSerializerIsReflectionEnabledByDefault=true' and Roslyn 5.6.0 pinned to match the extractor; run with 'dotnet run AttributeCensus.cs -- <root>'.

nodes.summary: The Lightroom Classic SDK API as a queryable JSON index: 909 members across 65 namespaces (SDK 15.3), each with signature, summary, params, return value, and the "first supported in version" stamp. Query with script.search-json (-Query scored search, -Where name=photo:setRawMetadata exact lookup); schema via Read-JsonCache -Schema. Built from the LuaDoc HTML the SDK ships by C:\repos\ImageSelectorV2\tools\Build-LightroomApiIndex.ps1; sibling indexes lightroom-api-8.0.json (815 members) and lightroom-api-3.0.json (677) beside it answer "when did this API appear" beyond the since field. Source corpus: the three SDK folders under C:\Users\lori_\Documents\LR-Lua\LR-Lua.
caveats: Derived data: rebuild with Build-LightroomApiIndex.ps1 after dropping in a new SDK; nothing detects a stale index.
Param descriptions flatten LuaDoc's nested key lists (setRawMetadata's 30 recognized keys become one prose string) -- the structure is in the HTML if ever needed.
The builder lives in ImageSelectorV2, not JanetHome: it is Lightroom-specific, and the indexes live beside the corpus outside any repo.
memberCount counts namespace overview rows too (one per module, kind=namespace); functions and methods are memberCount minus moduleCount.

nodes.summary: Azure access tokens borrowed from the machine's `az login`, cached for the life of the process and served by both front ends (az_token, janet az token). The CLI has no cache of its own, so it BORROWS a running janet-mcp over HTTP -- 0.10s against 1.0s local -- starting one if none serves this graph, and falling back to local acquisition whenever that cannot be done. Answers with METADATA by default; the token itself is withheld unless raw is asked for, because an MCP tool result is written into a transcript that is persisted and re-sent every turn. 'servedBy' says which process worked it out. Scope takes an alias (arm, management, storage, graph, keyvault, sql, servicebus, cosmos) or a literal URI; a bare resource gains /.default. Format declared in contracts\az-token.schema.json, contract 2.
caveats: IT IS THE CLI'S SIGN-IN, NOT JANET'S. There is no service principal and no stored secret: AzureCliCredential shells out to `az account get-access-token`, so this works exactly when `az login` works and stops the moment that lapses. The token carries the access the signed-in user already has, which is why no scope allow-list is enforced -- refusing a scope here would remove no permission, it would only push the caller back to `az` and cost them the cache. Chosen deliberately on 2026-08-18 over DefaultAzureCredential (portable but its probe order surprises) and a service principal (no app registration exists, and it would introduce a secret to store).

THE CLI HAS NO CACHE OF ITS OWN AND NEVER WILL -- every invocation is a fresh process. It borrows a running janet-mcp instead (file.server-link), which is why 'servedBy' exists: cached:false from the CLI would otherwise be ambiguous between 'no server to ask' and 'the server's cache was cold'. Measured 2026-08-18: borrowed-and-warm 0.10s, local acquisition 0.47-1.6s depending on how warm `az` itself is, auto-launch-then-serve 1.74s. Use --local to force local work, --no-launch to use a server only if one is already up, --why to print which happened on stderr.

THERE IS NO --out-env, and the omission is deliberate rather than unfinished. A child process cannot set a variable in the shell that launched it, so such a flag could only print an assignment for the caller to eval -- which puts the token back on stdout, the exact thing it would exist to avoid. Use --out-file, or $env:AZ_TOKEN = janet az token --raw.

The 'token' key is ABSENT rather than null when it was not requested. Absent says 'you did not ask'; null would say 'there is no token', and those want different actions from whoever hit the difference. Do not 'fix' it into a nullable field -- the contract requires the other keys and deliberately does not require this one.

GET /az/token ON A RUNNING SERVER HANDS A BEARER TOKEN TO ANY LOCAL PROCESS THAT ASKS. That is the same access a local process already has by running `az account get-access-token` itself, so the trust boundary is unchanged -- but it is unchanged ONLY because the server binds 127.0.0.1 and nothing else. Binding this server to any other interface would turn a loopback convenience into a token oracle; the endpoint would have to grow authentication in the same change.

A SERVER OLDER THAN THIS ENDPOINT ANSWERS /health AND 404s /az/token, and the CLI then falls back to local work SILENTLY. Correct, and invisible: the only symptom is that a borrowed call is unaccountably slow. --why names the port and says the server did not answer. Rotate the server (Update-McpServer.ps1) after taking this change.

THE CONTRACT GATE CANNOT CHECK THIS FORMAT ON A MACHINE WITHOUT `az login`. Its sampler is the only one in Test-OutputContracts.ps1 that depends on the environment rather than the repo; it reports skipped, which is neither a pass nor a failure. A green run on a build agent is NOT evidence that this envelope matches its schema. Verified both ways on 2026-08-18, the skip by pointing AZURE_CONFIG_DIR at an empty directory.

The unit tests never touch Azure and never start a server -- they drive a stub credential, a controlled clock, and a port nothing serves. That is deliberate, so they do not assert the machine's state. What it leaves unproven: the AzureCliCredential wiring, and the auto-launch path. Both were exercised by hand on 2026-08-18 (launch verified by killing the server and watching the next CLI call bring one back from .janet-bin\current); nothing re-checks either automatically.

Azure.Identity 1.21.0 ships its net10.0 lib as a 17KB facade that FORWARDS all 56 public types into Azure.Core. Reflection over the file reports zero types, and so does `janet assembly` -- correctly, but it reads exactly like a broken lookup. Resolve through GetForwardedTypes(), or introspect Azure.Core instead. The package's XML doc file is a 156-byte stub with no members, so `janet api` has nothing to say about it either.

nodes.summary: Lets the CLI borrow a running janet-mcp instead of repeating its work: resolves the port the way the server does (.mcp.json first, derivation only as a bootstrap), probes /health, starts a server from .janet-bin\current or PATH when none serves this graph, and fetches a path over loopback HTTP. Every failure path returns "do it yourself" rather than throwing, because the CLI exists so hooks and shells have something that works WITHOUT a server. A server identified by port alone is the bug this avoids: identity is the graph it serves, which is why /health carries the graph path. Used today only by `janet az token` -- the one place a fresh process pays for state it cannot keep.
caveats: NOT A GENERAL FORWARDING LAYER, and deliberately not one yet. Only `janet az token` routes through it. Making every CLI verb forward would fix the version skew note.janet-mcp-port and script.ensure-mcp-server both warn about (a stale global CLI answering differently from the server), and it is the 'elect one owner' half of the parked shared-state thread item -- but it would also mean the CLI stopped being the thing that works when the server is down, which is the entire reason the CLI exists. Decide that on purpose, not by extending this to one more verb at a time.

IT STARTS A DAEMON AS A SIDE EFFECT. `janet az token` with no server running spawns a detached janet-mcp that outlives the command, by design and at Lori's request. A caller that must not do this passes --no-launch; a caller that wants nothing to do with a server passes --local. Worth remembering before wiring this verb into a hook that runs on every file write.

The child is started with its streams LEFT ALONE -- not redirected. Redirecting and not draining is how a child deadlocks once a pipe buffer fills (the same failure Janet.Mcp's stdio logging comment describes), and draining would mean a short-lived CLI process babysitting a server meant to outlive it. The cost is that the server's startup errors go wherever the CLI's console went.

The start wait is bounded at 5s and a timeout is NOT a failure to start: the server may still come up and serve the next call. The current call falls back to local work. So a first invocation on a cold machine can legitimately report servedBy:process while leaving a healthy server behind it.

PROBE FAILURE MEANS FREE, NOT FOREIGN -- inherited from Health, and load-bearing here for a different reason: this class treats 'not obviously a janet-mcp for my graph' as a reason to work locally. A server that is genuinely there but slow to answer /health (500ms timeout) is therefore skipped rather than waited for, which is the right trade for a CLI and would be the wrong one for a supervisor.

Not covered by any test that starts a real server. The unit tests point it at a port nothing serves and assert the fallback; the launch path was exercised by hand on 2026-08-18. A test that spawned a daemon from the suite would leave one behind on failure, which is worse than the gap.

nodes.summary: Checks that drive-absolute paths in CLIENT config (.mcp.json commands, settings.json permission rules) still resolve, and suggests replacements by deepest shared path suffix. The gap Invoke-JanetStartup leaves: it validates the manifest's own entries, not the config files a session actually depends on.
caveats: Only DRIVE-ABSOLUTE paths are checked. A relative rule resolves against whichever project dir the session launched in, which is unknowable here, and guessing would produce false accusations against rules that work.

Route findings into their own captured field, NEVER into the brief's problems: Start-Janet gates launch on problems, and this fires legitimately from a foreign project dir -- the exact 2026-08-01 regression that broke launching from anywhere but JanetHome.
Reports and proposes, never rewrites. Repairing a permission allow-list is a privilege change and stays a deliberate act.
Resolution is existence only: a path that resolves to a stale flat copy instead of the intended .mcp-bin\current junction still reports ok.

WIRED INTO THE STARTUP MANIFEST 2026-09-01 as the fourth run entry, captureAs 'configPaths' -- captured, never a problem, so a foreign-dir launch still succeeds (verified from C:\repos\RetirementCore: 5 files scanned, 2 absolute paths, ok:true, 0 problems). In JanetHome's own config it finds zero drive-absolute paths, so the entry only earns its keep where a .mcp.json or settings file carries one; it costs about 100 ms per start.

nodes.summary: janet check reported 426/426 passing, exit 0, succeeded true, while one of three test assemblies had run 4 of its 131 tests. NOT a contract limitation -- a defect in the check. Reproduced 2026-08-30: raw 'dotnet test' EXITS 1 and prints 'The active test run was aborted. Reason: Test host process crashed' with the exception and source line; janet check exits 0, asserts succeeded true, emits nothing on stderr, and replaces the crashed assembly with a phantom entry named after the TRX FILENAME reporting 0/0. Three failures, all in the wrapper: the runner's non-zero exit is swallowed, the abort message is discarded entirely, and a partial TRX is mis-parsed into a filename-named assembly instead of being reported as aborted. The tell WAS in the envelope -- a .trx-named assembly at 0/0 -- unlabelled, and misread as formatting clutter for hours. Fix in order: propagate the runner's exit code (this alone catches it), surface the abort text as a field, stop emitting filename-named assemblies. A discovery pass (dotnet test --list-tests --no-build, 2.8s for 131 tests) is worth having for a DIFFERENT failure -- tests never discovered via a filter typo or missing attribute, where nothing aborts and nothing is non-zero -- and conflating the two was part of the original wrong diagnosis. Lesson: a tool summarising another tool must propagate its verdict, not recompute one from the parts it managed to parse; 'succeeded' was derived from 'no failures in the results I could read', which is equally true of a crash and an empty set.
caveats: The first version of this note diagnosed it as a structural blind spot in CONTRACT 4 and proposed a baseline-plus-discovery scheme. That was wrong, written from reading the schema instead of running the failing case, and is corrected here. The schema was not the problem.
Reproduced on one runner (VSTest/xUnit, net10.0) and one crash mode (test host death). Whether every abort path exits non-zero and prints the same banner is unverified.
The discovery-pass idea survives only for undiscovered tests, which is a separate failure from this one.

FIXED 2026-08-30, envelope contract 5: runnerExitCode propagates the runner's verdict into succeeded and the exit code, tests.abort carries the banner, and partial TRX entries (nameless, counterless, or outcome=Aborted) are labelled status 'aborted' instead of phantom 0/0 assemblies. Verified by re-running this note's reproduction: the same crash now reports exit 1, succeeded false, and the Application..ctor line in tests.abort. The note's Fix section records the details; the discovery-pass idea for never-discovered tests remains open.

Independently re-verified 2026-08-30 after the contract 5 fix, from a separate session: same reproduction now yields exit 1, succeeded false, runnerExitCode 1, the full abort banner with the Application..ctor source line, and the partial TRX marked status aborted. Detection works. NEW FINDING from running it twice: the TRX takes DIFFERENT SHAPES across runs of the identical crash -- once as 'RetirementCore.App.Tests: 3/3' (named itself, carried counters) and once as a filename-named entry at 0/0 (too partial to name anything), decided by how far the host got before dying. The aborted detection catches both, but the consequence is that a status:aborted entry CANNOT RELIABLY NAME THE ASSEMBLY that died -- in the filename case the real assembly is absent from the list entirely. That looks inherent rather than fixable: a name the TRX never recorded is not recoverable from it. The abort banner is the channel that answers 'whose', since it carries the source file and line; status:aborted answers only 'one did'. The two are not interchangeable.

nodes.summary: Captures a running application's window to a PNG so an agent can SEE what it drew. Launches an exe (or attaches by -ProcessId), waits for its first titled window, brings it forward, and saves the client area; -FullWindow captures the frame too. Exists because an agent session cannot look at a window, so "does it render correctly" otherwise degrades to "it started and did not crash" -- a claim a viewer drawing nothing at all passes. Three defaults were learned by getting them wrong, and each wrong answer looked confident rather than failing: match by PROCESS ID not title (title matching silently captured an unrelated window that merely had the app name in its caption), require a NON-EMPTY title (a console-subsystem exe owns a console window too, and MainWindowHandle can resolve to it), and declare PER-MONITOR DPI AWARENESS before any coordinate call (a DPI-unaware process gets virtualized coordinates, so ClientToScreen points somewhere else entirely on a scaled display). JSON envelope by default with width/height/origin/title/waitedMs, -Text for a terminal; exit 1 on failure. Kills a launched process unless -KeepRunning; never kills an attached one.
caveats: Uses CopyFromScreen, which grabs the SCREEN region rather than the window's own backing store -- so the window is brought to the foreground first, and ANYTHING OVERLAPPING IT IS CAPTURED INSTEAD. Do not run two captures concurrently, and do not trust a capture taken while a dialog or notification was on top. PrintWindow with PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT would capture an occluded window, but it returns BLACK for GPU-presented content (Direct3D, OpenGL, raylib), which is exactly the content this script exists to look at -- hence the trade.

-SettleMilliseconds defaults to 1200 because a GPU-rendered window can present its first real frame several frames after it becomes visible; capturing too early yields a blank or half-drawn image that looks like a rendering bug. Raise it for a slow-starting app rather than concluding the app is broken.
Windows-only: the whole thing is user32 P/Invoke. There is no cross-platform equivalent here.

Verified 2026-08-31 against a raylib viewer (996x607 client, correct content confirmed by reading the PNG back) and against a WPF window hosting a Direct3D 11 surface through D3DImage -- GPU-presented content captures correctly, which is the case PrintWindow would have failed.

nodes.summary: Diffs two PNGs and reports the count, the ratio, the maximum per-channel delta, and the BOUNDING BOX of the differences. The other half of Get-WindowCapture.ps1: capture answers what it looks like, this answers whether it changed. The bounding box is the field that earns its place -- a count says something moved, a box says whether it was the thing you touched or the corner of the window, and those want different reactions. -Tolerance absorbs compositing and antialiasing noise, -MaxDifferingRatio turns it into a gate (exit 1), -DiffFile writes differing pixels in red over a dimmed copy of the reference. Comparison runs over locked bits rather than GetPixel, which is the difference between milliseconds and seconds on a 600k-pixel image. JSON envelope by default, -Text for a terminal.
caveats: AN EXACT-ZERO THRESHOLD IS USUALLY WRONG FOR WINDOW CAPTURES. Windows 11 rounds window corners and composites the desktop through them, so a captured window's corner pixels carry whatever was behind it. Measured twice on 2026-08-31, on a 996x607 client area of the same unchanged application: 31 then 29 differing pixels of 604,572, max channel delta 2, every one inside a 10x10 patch at ONE corner. Read the bounding box before believing a small non-zero count is a regression, or pass -Tolerance 4.

Dimension mismatch is an error, not a difference -- it exits 1 with the two sizes rather than trying to align or scale. Comparing a resized capture would report a difference at every pixel and mean nothing.
Alpha is ignored deliberately: a screen capture is opaque and its alpha channel carries no information. Two images differing ONLY in alpha compare as identical.

The visual-golden trap is the same one note.golden-tests records for text goldens: a reference image regenerated from the current build agrees with the current build by construction. Capture the reference from the code as it stood BEFORE the change -- a git worktree of the prior commit is the cheap way -- and edit it deliberately when behaviour is meant to change.

nodes.summary:
Finds screenshots wherever Windows and OneDrive have actually put them, so "the user mentioned a screenshot, where is it" stops being a guessing game. Resolves the Screenshots KNOWN FOLDER from the registry (KNOWNFOLDERID_Screenshots, {B7BEDE81-DF94-4682-A7D8-57A52620B86F}, under User Shell Folders), adds the OneDrive and local Pictures/Desktop/Downloads roots, prunes roots nested inside other roots, and searches by DEPTH rather than by folder name -- because the name is localised and OneDrive suffixes duplicates. Filters by -Name substring (a pasted full filename or just the time digits both work) and -WithinHours, newest first. Reports the roots it searched alongside the hits, since "nothing found" and "nothing found in the wrong places" are otherwise indistinguishable. -IncludeVideos adds the Game Bar capture folder. JSON envelope by default, -Text for a terminal; exit 1 on no match.</summary>
<parameter name="parameters">["Name", "WithinHours", "First", "SearchDepth", "Path", "IncludeVideos", "Text", "Pretty"]
caveats: WRITTEN BECAUSE GUESSING FAILED, 2026-08-31. Pictures\Screenshots, Desktop and Downloads were all tried and all missed; the file was in OneDrive\Pictures\Screenshots 1 -- with a space and a digit, because OneDrive made a second folder during a sync conflict. An exact-name match on 'Screenshots' finds nothing, and a %USERPROFILE%-relative guess misses entirely once OneDrive has redirected Pictures.

NESTED ROOTS DOUBLE-REPORT, and they nest by default: the registry known folder resolves to <OneDrive>\Pictures\Screenshots, which sits inside the Pictures root. The first version deduplicated only identical paths and reported every hit twice (measured: 58 matches where there were 41). Roots are now sorted shortest-first so an ancestor subsumes its children, and results are deduplicated by path as well, in case a junction puts one file under two roots that do not look nested.

SearchDepth defaults to 2, which reaches Pictures\Screenshots 1\ without walking a whole photo library. A screenshot filed deeper needs -SearchDepth raised; a large Pictures tree wants -Name or -WithinHours to keep the listing useful rather than the search fast, since the walk happens either way.
Windows-only: known folders are a registry concept and there is no cross-platform equivalent. On a machine with no OneDrive the OneDrive roots are simply skipped rather than erroring.

Matches by file extension, not by content or provenance, so any png or jpg in those roots is a candidate -- a photo library under Pictures will match a bare -First query. It finds FILES that could be screenshots, not screenshots specifically.

THE TRIGGER IS OFTEN A BARE FILENAME WITH NO IMAGE. In Claude Code a user attaching a screenshot can arrive as a message whose entire content is the file name -- 'Screenshot 2026-09-02 161433.png' -- with no image the model can see. That is not an empty message and not a request to guess; it is this script's cue, and the time digits alone work as -Name. Once found, the Read tool renders the PNG, so the whole round trip is two calls. Observed 2026-09-02, when the model instead hand-rolled a Get-ChildItem sweep over six guessed roots -- which happened to work and should not have been written, because this script already existed and the catalog was not queried first.

nodes.summary: Manifest run entry that makes sure the razorgraph-mcp HTTP server is up on 7718. A thin forwarder to Ensure-McpServer.ps1 with razorgraph's parameters, so the probe/start/staleness logic exists once; it emits that script's JSON envelope unchanged. Added 2026-08-31, when this repo's .mcp.json was found to declare razorgraph alongside janet while startup ensured only janet -- so razorgraph's tools could be silently absent with every startup gate green.
caveats: IT EXISTS ONLY BECAUSE A MANIFEST 'cmd' IS A BARE PATH. Invoke-JanetStartup validates run entries with Test-Path -PathType Leaf and has nowhere to put an argument list, so a per-server wrapper is the cheapest way to reach a parameterised script. Do not copy the probe/start logic into it -- that is the duplication this shape avoids.

-Repo defaults to C:\repos\RazorGraphTool, a MACHINE-SPECIFIC path. On a checkout elsewhere the forward reports state no-server-binary rather than failing, which is truthful but will read as a permanent red in the brief until the default is corrected or the parameter is passed.

Passes -ServerArgument explicitly BECAUSE razorgraph-mcp takes no --base: it is told which solution to graph per call, not per process. Inheriting Ensure-McpServer's janet default would make the server exit at startup.
The port is duplicated between this default (7718), the -ServerArgument it builds, and the url in .mcp.json. They must agree; nothing checks that they do.

nodes.summary: Calls one tool on an MCP server over HTTP and hands back its parsed payload, so a script can ask the graph or the catalog a question directly instead of going through a CLI twin or a saved-graph file. Written 2026-09-01 after measuring that "hooks run as separate processes and cannot speak MCP" is true only of STDIO -- a stdio server is a child process the client owns, but an HTTP server is a port and anything can dial it. Both janet (7717) and razorgraph (7718) are HTTP today, so both are script-reachable now. Handles the three things that make the naive attempt fail: responses are SSE-framed rather than bare JSON, the session id arrives as an Mcp-Session-Id header that every later request must echo, and the handshake needs a notifications/initialized between initialize and the first tools/call. Unwraps twice by default -- out of the JSON-RPC envelope and out of the text content block -- so a tool returning JSON comes back as an object; -Raw stops at the text for tools that return prose. -ListTools is a cheap liveness and surface check.
caveats: INVOKE-RESTMETHOD DOES NOT WORK HERE, and that is the whole reason this script is thirty lines rather than three. The body arrives as 'event: message' then 'data: {json}', so Invoke-RestMethod hands back a string that looks like a broken response. Use Invoke-WebRequest and pull the data: lines -- both framings are accepted, so a server answering plain application/json also works.

Only tools/call and tools/list are implemented. Resources, prompts, sampling, progress notifications and cancellation are not, and a long-running tool is simply waited on -- hence the 120s default TimeoutSec, which build_solution can still exceed on a large solution.

A protocol error (unknown tool, bad arguments) and a tool-level failure (isError on the result) are reported differently on purpose: the first is a JSON-RPC error object, the second is a normal result carrying isError. Collapsing them would hide which one happened. Both exit 1.

The session is not reused across invocations -- every call performs a fresh handshake. That costs a round trip per call and is irrelevant for a report that makes a handful of calls, but a loop over hundreds of nodes should batch through one tool call (research with many focusIds) rather than calling this per node.

VERIFIED AGAINST BOTH SERVERS 2026-09-01, which matters because they are different implementations: RazorGraph.Mcp 1.0.0.0 on 7718 (25 tools, graph_summary) and janet-mcp 0.1.0.0 on 7717 (14 tools, research_query). Same handshake, same SSE framing, same session header on both. protocolVersion is sent as the literal 2025-06-18 rather than negotiated down, so a server wanting an older version has not been tested.

The default Uri is razorgraph (7718) because that is what the first caller needed. Pass -Uri http://127.0.0.1:7717/ for janet. Nothing checks that the server behind a given port is the one you meant, so a wrong port reports 'unknown tool' rather than 'wrong server'.

nodes.summary: Reports types whose members split into groups that share no state -- connected-component cohesion (the LCOM4 shape) computed from the code graph's Reads/Writes and sibling Calls edges rather than from source. Two members are linked if they touch a common field or one calls the other; two or more components means the members partition into clusters that never meet. Exists because a divergence in BACKING STATE between members used together is invisible at the call site and obvious in the graph: in GameHub, GroupOps.IsClaimed reads the system-wide claim cache while ClaimantOf reads the group's own member list, GatherDoctrine.ReconcilePass treats them as a matched pair, and with two concurrent groups the second question answers "nobody" about a cell the first said was taken -- so the squatter swap never fires and a unit is stranded. Five adversarial reviewers and a night of reading found that once; this prints it as one row. Calls the graph live through script.invoke-mcp-tool, so there is no saved-graph step and no staleness question.
caveats: IT CANNOT TELL A BUG FROM A DESIGN, because the graph cannot say whether two roots are semantically alternatives for the same information. _system and _group are both 'where claim state lives', which is what made their divergence a defect; a type genuinely holding two unrelated responsibilities reports identically and is a refactor. Read the clusters before believing either story. Measured on Nav.Core: 3 of 48 types reported, of which one is the real bug and two (Movement, Terrain) are benign static-utility splits.

TWO FILTERS DO ALL THE NOISE REDUCTION, and without them the report is useless -- the first run flagged 44 of 48 types. (1) Members touching no field are excluded from the component count: an auto-property or a positional record member reads no field the graph can see, because the backing field is compiler-generated and absent, so every record otherwise reports as N singleton clusters. (2) Const fields are not state: counting them links every static helper reading the same literal and reports a parser as split from the type it parses.
Constructors are excluded deliberately. A constructor writes every field, so leaving it in merges every cluster and the answer is always 'cohesive'.

GROUP-OBJECT RETURNING ONE GROUP HANDS BACK A BARE GROUPINFO, whose own .Count is the number of items IN the group -- so an unwrapped $groups.Count read 6 members as 6 clusters and reported BinaryHeap, which has exactly one. The @() around it is not optional. Found by the first sweep printing a cluster count that disagreed with the clusters it printed.

Static analysis only: a field reached through a property accessor, through reflection, or by a method call that mutates a collection is invisible here, and note.razorgraph-mcp-server records that Writes detection is assignment-syntax only. Absence of a shared field is not proof of independence.
Scope it with -Project. Across a whole solution the answer means little, because cohesion is a per-assembly judgement.

nodes.summary: The work moved to a DIFFERENT MACHINE, not a different drive, and that distinction is the point: a drive rename means D:\Repos\X became C:\repos\X and find-and-replace closes it, while a machine move means some things are not here at all and no path rewrite reaches them. Absolute paths naming the old machine sat dead in the catalog and in a permission allow-list for weeks without failing once. Swept 2026-09-01: five catalog nodes corrected, and two dead rules in RetirementCore\.claude\settings.json repointed at C:\repos\lorithantos\JanetHome\scripts\Get-Research.ps1. RazorGraphTool and ImageSelectorV2 were carried over so their paths were merely wrong; DriveSurvey is absent from this machine AND from GitHub under six guessed names (ImageSelectorV2 resolves from the same shell, so that is a real absence, not an auth failure), so its path was REMOVED rather than guessed and recovering it needs a remote only Lori has. Three silent-failure shapes recorded: a path inside prose is read rather than resolved so nothing checks it; an allow-list entry for a nonexistent path is never consulted and surfaces only as an unexpected prompt long after the cause; and an existence check standing in for a correctness check.

GameHub keeps its design history in C:\repos\gamehub\docs\ rather than in doc comments, split by TENSE: present tense (what this does, what a caller can get wrong) stays in the XML comment next to the code; past tense (what it replaced, what was tried, what was measured) moves to docs and is referenced from the remarks it was cut from. The property that makes this worth doing is that a past-tense claim needs no maintenance -- "on a 512x384 map that is 62% wall it found nothing" is permanently true of the code that existed that day -- while a comment carrying it sits in the tooltip forever describing a class that no longer exists. Four files: gates-and-regions.md (why ChokepointScan was replaced, the 90-regions/median-8/largest-46% partition and what merging and splitting were worth, the link-graph route measurement that had to be rebuilt); search-and-movement.md (field following, arena-200 586/5.52M -> 388/1.66M, the FollowBlockedTicks sweep, the generation-stamp measurement banded by path length, and the traces that changed a rule); scale-and-doctrine.md (the 60Hz derived-accident calibration, the repair reserve inverting to lowest-rank-first, last-hit attribution measured unbiased); viewer.md (the viewer goes dark rather than failing at scale; why replay compositing was reverted). Enforced at the other end by Directory.Build.props turning on GenerateDocumentationFile, so a stale cref or param is a build warning rather than prose above a member.
caveats: Lives in a DIFFERENT REPO from this catalog: the path is absolute (C:\repos\gamehub\docs) rather than JanetHome-relative, so path validation here does not check it.

The tense rule decides what MOVES, not what is short. RepairPolicy's remarks are ~50 lines and stay, because every line of them is present-tense doctrine rather than history -- length alone is not the fault the rule addresses.

docs/ is written by hand and nothing checks it against the code. It is safe only because it holds claims about the past, which cannot go stale; a present-tense claim that leaks in there is exactly the drift the split was meant to avoid.
